      A Anyone who has spent a day at the seaside has seen the water creep up the beach and then retreat again. Along most coasts this happens twice a day, and the cause lies 384,000 kilometres away. The gravity of the Moon pulls on the Earth, and because water moves easily, the oceans bulge slightly towards the Moon. A second bulge forms on the opposite side of the planet. As the Earth rotates, a coastline passes through both bulges, producing two high tides and two low tides roughly every twenty-five hours.

      B The Sun also influences the tides, though its effect is less than half that of the Moon because it is so much farther away. When the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line, at full moon and new moon, their forces combine to create especially large tides called spring tides. The name has nothing to do with the season. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, the result is the weaker neap tide.

      C The shape of the coast makes an enormous difference. In the open ocean the water rises by less than a metre, but in narrow bays it can be funnelled to great heights. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada the difference between high and low tide can exceed fifteen metres.

      D The tides have a slow but measurable effect on the planet itself. As the bulges of water drag across the sea floor, friction acts as a brake on the Earth's rotation, and each century the day grows longer by about two thousandths of a second. The evidence is preserved in fossil corals, which add a thin layer of limestone every day; specimens 400 million years old show that a year then contained about 400 days, each lasting less than twenty-two hours. The energy lost by the Earth is transferred to the Moon, which is moving away from us by almost four centimetres a year.

      E For the plants and animals of the shore, the tide is the main fact of life. The strip of coast that is covered and uncovered twice a day is one of the harshest environments on Earth: its inhabitants must survive drying wind, hot sun and fresh rainwater, and then the pounding of waves. Mussels and barnacles close their shells tightly when the water retreats and open them to feed when it returns. Many sea creatures time their breeding by the tides, coming ashore to lay their eggs only on the nights of the highest spring tides.

      F People who misjudge the tide can pay heavily. When Julius Caesar landed in Britain in 55 BC, his soldiers, who were used to the almost tideless Mediterranean, pulled their ships onto the beach. A few nights later a spring tide combined with a storm filled the ships with water and smashed many of them. Even today, rescue services are regularly called out to walkers who have been cut off by water rising behind them across flat sands.

      G Tides have long been useful to people. Fishermen and sailors plan their work around them, and tidal mills were grinding grain in Europe over a thousand years ago. Today engineers are building turbines that generate electricity from tidal currents, a source of energy that, unlike wind, is entirely predictable.

      A Bamboo looks like a tree, but botanically it is a grass. There are well over a thousand species, ranging from plants a few centimetres tall to giants that reach thirty metres. Most grow in the warm, wet regions of Asia, South America and Africa. Bamboo is famous for its speed: under ideal conditions certain species can grow almost a metre in a single day, faster than any other plant.

      B A bamboo stem is hollow and divided into sections by solid joints. This structure makes it both light and extremely strong; weight for weight, it can resist stretching better than steel. In much of Asia it has been used for centuries to build houses, bridges and furniture, and in Hong Kong workers still construct bamboo scaffolding around skyscrapers.

      C Few plants have served people in so many ways. Before paper became common, Chinese writers used narrow strips of bamboo tied together with string, and the plant has supplied Asia with water pipes, fishing rods, musical instruments and chopsticks. It even played a part in the history of electric light. In 1880, searching for a material that would glow for a long time without burning away, the American inventor Thomas Edison tested thousands of plant fibres and found that a thread of carbonised Japanese bamboo lasted for more than 1,200 hours. Bamboo was used in his lamps for the next decade.

      D The secret of the plant's rapid growth lies underground. Bamboo spreads by means of horizontal stems beneath the soil, from which new shoots rise each spring, so that an entire grove may be a single plant. A shoot emerges from the ground already as thick as it will ever be and reaches its full height within about two months; after that it hardens but grows no further. The dense network of roots holds soil in place and is valued for preventing erosion on steep slopes. In gardens, however, the same habit makes some kinds of bamboo extremely difficult to control.

      E Bamboo is also eaten. The young shoots are a popular vegetable across East Asia, although most kinds must be boiled first to remove bitter, mildly poisonous substances. For the giant panda, bamboo is practically the whole menu. Because the plant contains so little nourishment, an adult panda has to eat for as long as twelve hours a day, consuming more than twelve kilograms of leaves and stems.

      F One of the plant's strangest features is the way it flowers. Many species flower only once, after several decades, and then die. Remarkably, all the plants of the same species often flower in the same year, even when they are growing on different continents. For animals that depend on bamboo, the result can be disastrous. Giant pandas, which eat almost nothing else, have starved when the bamboo in their area died off.

      G Bamboo is now attracting interest as an environmentally friendly material. It can be harvested after three to five years, compared with decades for most timber, and it grows back from its roots without replanting. It is being turned into flooring, paper and fabric. Critics point out, however, that producing soft bamboo fabric usually requires strong chemicals, so the finished product is not always as green as its label suggests.

      A We tend to think of memory as a kind of video recording that can be played back whenever we wish. Psychologists have shown that this picture is wrong. Remembering is an active process of reconstruction, and each time we recall an event we rebuild it, sometimes adding details that were never there.

      B Researchers usually distinguish three stages. Sensory memory holds what we see and hear for a second or two. A small part of this passes into short-term memory, which can keep about seven items for less than half a minute unless we repeat them. Only information that is rehearsed, or that matters to us emotionally, is transferred to long-term memory, where it may last a lifetime.

      C The German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus studied forgetting in the 1880s by memorising lists of meaningless syllables. He found that most forgetting happens very quickly, within the first day, and then slows down. He also discovered that reviewing material at increasing intervals, a technique now called spaced repetition, is far more effective than studying it many times in one session.

      D Much of what is known about where memories are formed comes from a single patient. In 1953 a young American, Henry Molaison, underwent an operation to cure severe epilepsy, in which surgeons removed a small structure deep in the brain called the hippocampus. The epilepsy improved, but for the remaining fifty-five years of his life he was unable to form new long-term memories; he greeted the doctors who studied him as strangers every day. Yet he could still learn physical skills, such as drawing a shape while watching his hand in a mirror, without any recollection of having practised. Memory, it became clear, is not one system but several.

      E The hippocampus can also change with use. To obtain a licence, London taxi drivers must learn the layout of some 25,000 streets, a task that takes three or four years. When the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire scanned their brains in 2000, she found that the rear part of the hippocampus was larger than in other people, and largest in those who had been driving longest.

      F Ordinary people can improve their memories considerably with technique. The oldest method, attributed to the Greek poet Simonides, is to imagine a familiar building and place the items to be remembered in different rooms; to recall them, one simply takes a walk through the building in the mind. Competitors in modern memory championships use this approach to memorise the order of a pack of playing cards in under half a minute. Tests suggest that such people are not born with unusual brains: they have simply trained.

      G Because memories are rebuilt, they can be distorted. In a well-known experiment by Elizabeth Loftus, people watched a film of a car accident. Those who were later asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other gave higher estimates than those who heard the word 'hit', and some even remembered broken glass that had not been shown. Such findings have made courts more cautious about relying on the testimony of eyewitnesses.

      A Before paper existed, people wrote on whatever was available: clay tablets in Mesopotamia, papyrus in Egypt, and bamboo strips or silk in China. Each had drawbacks. Bamboo was heavy, silk was costly, and papyrus cracked easily in damp climates.

      B According to Chinese tradition, paper was invented in AD 105 by Cai Lun, an official at the imperial court. He is said to have soaked tree bark, old rags and fishing nets in water, beaten them into a pulp and spread the mixture on a screen to dry. Archaeologists have since found fragments of paper that are two centuries older, so Cai Lun probably improved an existing method rather than creating it. Even so, his version was cheap and light, and it spread rapidly through China.

      C For several hundred years the technique remained in East Asia. Its journey westwards is traditionally linked to a battle near the Talas River in Central Asia in 751, after which captured Chinese papermakers are said to have taught their craft in Samarkand. The city soon became famous for its fine paper. From there the knowledge passed to Baghdad, Cairo and, by the twelfth century, to Spain.

      D Europeans at first distrusted the new material, considering it less durable than parchment, which was made from animal skin. Opinions changed when printing with movable type appeared in the fifteenth century. A single large Bible on parchment required the skins of about 170 calves; paper made mass production possible. Books became cheaper, literacy rose, and ideas began to travel faster than ever before.

      E For centuries paper in Europe was made almost entirely from old linen and cotton rags, and as printing expanded, the supply could not keep up. Rag collectors went from door to door, and some governments banned the export of rags altogether. The solution had been suggested as early as 1719 by a French scientist, René de Réaumur, who noticed that wasps build their nests from a kind of paper made by chewing wood. It was not until the 1840s, however, that a German weaver, Friedrich Keller, built a machine that ground logs into pulp. Within a few decades wood had replaced rags, and the price of paper fell sharply.

      F Cheap paper changed society once again. Daily newspapers selling for a penny, popular novels, school exercise books and paper bags all date from this period. But the new material had a hidden weakness. Chemicals used in making it left the paper slightly acidic, and over the years the acid attacks the fibres. Books printed between about 1850 and 1990 turn yellow and brittle, and libraries around the world now face the enormous task of treating or copying millions of volumes before they crumble.

      G In the 1970s, as computers entered offices, it was widely predicted that paper would soon be unnecessary. The opposite happened: with a printer on every desk, the consumption of office paper rose for the next thirty years, and has only recently begun to decline. Meanwhile the growth of online shopping has greatly increased the demand for cardboard packaging. Today well over half of the paper used in Europe is collected and recycled, although the fibres shorten each time and can be reused only a limited number of times.

      A The Silk Road was never a single road. It was a network of trade routes, stretching more than 6,000 kilometres, that linked China with the Mediterranean from about the second century BC. The name itself is modern: it was invented in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.

      B Few merchants travelled the whole distance. Goods were passed from one trader to another in a long chain, and their price rose at every stage. Silk went west, where wealthy Romans paid enormous sums for it, while glass, silver and wool moved east. Spices, paper, horses and precious stones were exchanged along the way. Caravans of camels crossed deserts and mountain passes, resting at roadside inns called caravanserais, which were built roughly a day's journey apart.

      C The opening of the route is usually credited to a Chinese official named Zhang Qian. In 138 BC the emperor sent him west to look for allies against the nomads who raided China's northern frontier. He was captured and held prisoner for ten years, but eventually escaped and returned home with detailed reports of rich kingdoms beyond the mountains. The emperor was particularly excited by his description of the powerful horses bred in the Fergana Valley, which were far superior to Chinese animals, and soon afterwards armies and merchants began to travel regularly to obtain them.

      D For centuries the Chinese kept the method of making silk a closely guarded secret, and revealing it to foreigners was punishable by death. Silk thread is unwound from the cocoons of a caterpillar that feeds only on the leaves of the mulberry tree. Customers in Rome had no idea of this, and one Roman writer assured his readers that silk was combed from the leaves of trees. According to a famous story, the monopoly was broken around AD 550, when two monks smuggled silkworm eggs out of Asia inside hollow walking sticks and presented them to the emperor in Constantinople.

      E The journey was hard and often dangerous. The most feared section skirted the Taklamakan Desert in what is now western China, where travellers faced sandstorms, extremes of heat and cold, and stretches of several days without water. Caravans kept to the string of oases around its edge. Bandits were a constant threat, so merchants travelled in large groups and paid local rulers for protection.

      F The great oasis cities of Central Asia, among them Samarkand, Bukhara and Merv, grew rich as meeting points. They were centres not only of commerce but also of learning, where scholars studied astronomy, medicine and mathematics. Ideas travelled as easily as goods. Buddhism reached China along these routes, and Islam later spread eastwards in the same way. Unfortunately, so did disease: many historians believe the plague that devastated Europe in the fourteenth century arrived along the trade routes from Asia.

      G The overland trade declined after the fifteenth century. European sailors found sea routes to Asia, and ships could carry far more cargo than camels at a lower cost. The old cities lost much of their importance, although their magnificent buildings still attract visitors today.

      C Around 1455 he completed his famous Bible, of which about 180 copies were printed. Sadly, Gutenberg did not profit from his work. He had borrowed heavily, and his business partner took him to court and gained control of the workshop.

      D The Bible itself was a remarkable piece of work. Each page has two columns of forty-two lines, set in a heavy type designed to imitate the handwriting of the best scribes, because Gutenberg wanted his product to look as much like a manuscript as possible. Spaces were left for coloured capital letters to be painted in afterwards by hand. Most copies were printed on paper, but about a quarter were on parchment for wealthier buyers. Around fifty copies survive today, and they are among the most valuable books in the world.

      E Producing a page was a slow business by modern standards. A compositor picked the metal letters one at a time from a case and arranged them, in mirror image, into lines. The finished page of type was locked in a frame, inked with leather pads, and pressed onto a sheet of damp paper. When enough copies had been printed, the type was taken apart and used again. Even so, a workshop with a single press could turn out more pages in a day than a scribe could copy in several months.

      F Not everyone welcomed the new art. Professional copyists saw their living disappear, and some scholars sneered at printed books as cheap and ugly; one Italian duke is said to have refused to allow a single one into his library. In 1492 a German abbot, Johannes Trithemius, wrote a pamphlet in praise of scribes, arguing that words written on parchment would last a thousand years while those printed on paper would soon perish. To make sure that his argument reached as many readers as possible, he had it printed.

      G The invention itself spread with extraordinary speed. By 1500 there were printing presses in more than 250 European towns, and millions of books had been produced. The effects were profound. Scientists could share accurate copies of their results, religious reformers could reach huge audiences, and ordinary languages such as German, French and English began to replace Latin in print. Some historians regard printing as the most important invention of the last thousand years.

      A The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC. It originally stood about 146 metres high and remained the tallest structure made by humans for nearly four thousand years. It contains roughly 2.3 million blocks of stone, most weighing more than two tonnes, and its sides are aligned almost perfectly with the points of the compass.

      B How such a monument was built without iron tools, wheels for heavy transport or cranes has fascinated people for centuries. The Greek writer Herodotus, who visited Egypt some two thousand years after the pyramid was finished, claimed that 100,000 slaves had worked on it. Modern archaeology tells a different story. Excavations near the site have revealed a workers' town with bakeries, breweries and even medical facilities. The builders were not slaves but paid labourers and farmers, perhaps 20,000 to 30,000 of them, who were well fed with bread, beer and meat.

      C Most of the limestone was cut in quarries close by. The finer white stone for the outer surface came from across the Nile, and granite for the inner chambers was floated down the river from Aswan, some 800 kilometres to the south. In 2013 archaeologists found the diary of an official named Merer, the oldest inscribed papyrus ever discovered, which describes boat crews delivering stone to Giza.

      D The blocks were probably dragged on wooden sledges up ramps made of mud brick and rubble. A wall painting shows a man pouring water on the sand in front of a sledge; experiments have confirmed that wet sand cuts the force needed to pull a heavy load by about half.

      E When it was completed, the pyramid looked very different from the stepped, sand-coloured monument that visitors see now. Its sides were covered with a smooth casing of polished white limestone, which must have shone brilliantly in the sun. Most of these stones were removed in the Middle Ages, after an earthquake in 1303 loosened them, and were reused to build the mosques and houses of Cairo. With the loss of the casing and of its topmost stones, the pyramid is now about eight metres shorter than when it was built.

      F The pyramid was intended to protect the king's body for ever, but in this it failed. Despite passages blocked with huge granite plugs, robbers broke in, probably within a few centuries, and when explorers entered the burial chamber in the ninth century they found only an empty stone coffin. One treasure did escape. In 1954 archaeologists clearing sand beside the pyramid discovered a sealed pit containing a cedar-wood boat, carefully taken apart into more than a thousand pieces. Reassembled, it is forty-three metres long and may have been meant to carry the king across the sky.

      G The building has not yet given up all its secrets. In 2017 an international team used detectors that register muons, particles from space which pass through stone, to make a kind of X-ray of the structure. They reported a previously unknown empty space at least thirty metres long above the main internal gallery. Its purpose is unknown, and since there is no passage leading to it, nobody has yet been able to look inside.

      A For most of history people had little need for exact time. Farmers rose with the sun and worked until dusk. The earliest timekeeping devices were shadow clocks: the Egyptians used tall stone obelisks, and later sundials, to divide the day into parts. These were useless at night or in cloudy weather, so water clocks were developed, in which water dripped at a steady rate from one container into another.

      B Mechanical clocks appeared in European monasteries and towns around 1300. They were driven by falling weights and had no minute hand, since they could gain or lose a quarter of an hour a day. A major advance came in 1656, when the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, reducing the error to a few seconds a day.

      C Accurate time was most urgently needed at sea. Sailors could find their latitude from the sun, but to calculate longitude they had to know the precise time at their home port, and pendulum clocks did not work on a rolling ship. After many shipwrecks the British government offered a large prize for a solution. It was eventually won by John Harrison, a self-taught carpenter, whose marine chronometer of 1759 lost only about five seconds on a voyage of several weeks.

      D Even then every town kept its own local time, set by the sun. It was the railways that forced a change, since timetables were impossible without a common standard. Britain adopted a single railway time in the 1840s, and in 1884 an international conference divided the world into time zones based on the line through Greenwich in London.

      E The twentieth century brought a new kind of accuracy. In 1927 an engineer at Bell Laboratories in the United States built a clock regulated by a crystal of quartz, which vibrates at a perfectly steady rate when an electric current passes through it. Early models filled a cabinet, but in 1969 a Japanese company put the technology into a wristwatch. Within a few years a cheap quartz watch kept better time than the finest mechanical one, and the traditional Swiss industry was thrown into crisis.

      F Greater precision still came from the atom. The first reliable atomic clock, built in Britain in 1955 by the physicist Louis Essen, counted the vibrations of caesium atoms. It was so much steadier than the rotation of the Earth that in 1967 scientists abandoned the old definition of the second as a fraction of a day and redefined it in terms of the caesium atom. The best modern clocks would lose less than one second in several billion years.

      G This precision has created a curious problem. The Earth does not turn at a perfectly constant speed, so time measured by atoms and time measured by the Sun slowly drift apart. Since 1972 an extra 'leap second' has occasionally been added to keep them together, twenty-seven so far. Because these adjustments can upset computer systems, international authorities voted in 2022 to stop making them by 2035.

      A At the height of its power the Roman Empire was held together by about 80,000 kilometres of paved roads, reaching from Britain to Syria. The famous saying that all roads lead to Rome was close to the truth: distances across the empire were measured from a golden milestone in the centre of the capital.

Roman engineers preferred straight lines, cutting through hills and bridging valleys rather than going around them. A trench was dug and filled with layers of sand, gravel and crushed stone, then topped with tightly fitted flat stones. The surface was slightly curved so that rainwater ran off into ditches at the sides.

      C Although designed for military purposes, the roads soon carried merchants, officials and ordinary travellers. Stone markers showed the distance to the next town, and inns stood at regular intervals.       D Roman engineers laid out their routes with a simple instrument called a groma, a pole carrying a horizontal cross from which four weighted strings hung. By lining up the strings with markers in the distance, surveyors could plot straight lines and right angles over many kilometres. Obstacles were met with ambitious structures. The bridge that carries the road across the River Tagus at Alcantara in Spain was completed in AD 106; it stands almost fifty metres above the water and is still in use.

      E Roads brought problems that sound surprisingly modern. By the first century BC the streets of Rome were so crowded that Julius Caesar banned most wheeled vehicles from the city during the hours of daylight. Deliveries therefore had to be made after dark, and the poet Juvenal complained that the rumble of carts through the narrow streets made sleep impossible. In towns such as Pompeii, raised stepping stones allowed pedestrians to cross without walking in the dirt, with gaps left between them for cart wheels.

      F Travellers planned their journeys with the help of written lists that named each stopping place and the distance to the next. A remarkable picture of the whole network survives in the so-called Peutinger Table, a medieval copy of a Roman map drawn on a strip of parchment nearly seven metres long but only thirty-four centimetres high. Shapes are wildly distorted, since the mapmaker cared only about the order of towns along each road, much as a modern diagram of an underground railway ignores true distances.

      G After the empire collapsed in the fifth century, the roads were no longer maintained, and many were robbed of their stone for other buildings. Yet their routes survived. A number of modern European highways follow exactly the lines that Roman surveyors laid out two thousand years ago.

      A A map is a way of seeing the world from above, something no human could actually do until the age of flight. The oldest known world map, a clay tablet from Babylon made around 600 BC, shows the earth as a flat disc surrounded by water, with Babylon itself at the centre. Placing one's own homeland in the middle is a habit that mapmakers have rarely abandoned.

      B The ancient Greeks took a more scientific approach. They knew the earth was a sphere, and in the second century AD Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, proposed a grid of lines of latitude and longitude to fix the position of any place. His work was forgotten in Europe for a thousand years but was preserved and improved by scholars in the Islamic world.

      C Medieval European maps were often religious pictures rather than practical guides, and they were of little use to sailors. This changed when voyages of exploration began. In 1569 the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator solved a serious problem for navigators: on his map a ship's constant compass course appeared as a straight line. The price was distortion. Because a globe cannot be flattened without stretching, regions far from the equator look much larger than they are. On a Mercator map Greenland seems about the same size as Africa, although Africa is in fact around fourteen times bigger.

      D Accuracy on land came later than at sea. The first survey of an entire country by precise measurement was carried out in France by four generations of the Cassini family and took more than a century to complete. Its early results showed that the coast lay considerably further east than earlier maps had suggested, and King Louis XIV is reported to have complained that his surveyors had cost him more territory than his enemies.

      E Maps have always been instruments of power as well as of knowledge. Portuguese and Spanish rulers treated their charts of newly explored coasts as state secrets. At a conference in Berlin in 1884 and 1885, European governments divided most of Africa among themselves, in many places simply by ruling straight lines across a map of regions that none of them had visited. Many of those lines, which cut through the lands of single peoples, remain national borders to this day.

      F Maps can also preserve mistakes. In 1798 an English mapmaker drew a great range of mountains, the Mountains of Kong, running across West Africa, on the strength of a single explorer's report. Other publishers copied it, and the range went on appearing in atlases for almost a century, until a French officer travelled through the region and found that it did not exist. Some modern publishers add small errors on purpose, such as an invented street, so that they can prove it when a rival copies their work.

      G Today satellites photograph every corner of the planet, and digital maps are updated daily. Yet a map is still a selection. Someone decides what to show and what to leave out, and those choices shape how we imagine the world.

      A For as long as people have gone to sea, they have needed guidance to reach harbour safely at night. The earliest signals were simply fires lit on hilltops. The most famous lighthouse of the ancient world was the Pharos of Alexandria in Egypt, completed around 280 BC. It was probably more than 100 metres tall, and it was counted among the seven wonders of the world. It guided ships for some 1,500 years before earthquakes finally brought it down.

      B Building on land was one thing; building on rocks out at sea was far harder. The Eddystone rocks off the south-west coast of England had wrecked countless ships when Henry Winstanley put up a wooden tower there in 1698. He was so confident of it that he wished to be inside during the greatest storm ever known. In 1703 he got his wish, and both tower and builder were swept away. The fourth Eddystone lighthouse, designed by John Smeaton in 1759, was made of interlocking blocks of granite and shaped like the trunk of an oak tree. It became the model for lighthouses everywhere.

      C Light was as much of a challenge as structure. Early lamps burned coal, candles or oil and were visible for only a few kilometres. In 1822 the French physicist Augustin Fresnel invented a lens made of rings of glass prisms, which gathered the light into a single powerful beam that could be seen more than thirty kilometres away.

      D A light is of little use unless the sailor knows which one he is looking at. From the early nineteenth century, therefore, each lighthouse was given its own signal: one might show a steady beam, another two flashes every ten seconds, a third alternate red and white. The effect was produced by rotating the lens with clockwork that the keeper had to wind by hand. By day, towers were told apart by their painted bands of colour, and in fog, when no light could be seen, by bells and later by powerful horns.

      E Among the greatest feats of lighthouse building was the tower on the Bell Rock, off the east coast of Scotland, a reef that lies under several metres of water at every high tide. The engineer Robert Stevenson and his men could work for only a few hours a day at low tide in summer, and the tower took from 1807 to 1810 to complete. It is still standing, the oldest surviving lighthouse built on a rock washed by the sea. Stevenson's descendants built lighthouses for over a century; one of them, Robert Louis Stevenson, abandoned the family profession to become a novelist.

      F Duty on such rocks demanded strong nerves. In 1801 one of the two keepers of the Smalls lighthouse, off the coast of Wales, died during a long storm. His companion, fearing that he would be accused of murder if the body disappeared, kept it lashed to the outside of the tower for weeks until a relief boat could land. He is said never to have recovered from the experience. From then on, British rock lighthouses were always manned by three keepers.

      G For centuries lighthouses were looked after by keepers, who lived in isolation for weeks on end. Automation has made the job disappear. Satellite navigation has reduced the need for lighthouses, yet most remain in service as a backup.

      A In hospitals around the world, computer programs are beginning to do work that was once reserved for highly trained specialists. The most striking progress has been in reading medical images. Software trained on hundreds of thousands of X-rays and scans can now detect signs of lung disease, breast cancer and eye conditions with an accuracy that, in several studies, matches that of experienced doctors.

      B These systems do not follow rules written by programmers. Instead they learn from examples. Shown a vast number of images that doctors have already labelled, the program gradually works out which patterns are associated with illness. This means that its quality depends heavily on its training data. A system taught mainly with images from one group of patients may perform poorly on others, a weakness that has already been observed with skin-cancer tools trained largely on photographs of light skin.

      C Supporters argue that the technology will not replace doctors but will free them from routine tasks. A program never gets tired, and it can check thousands of scans overnight, flagging the urgent ones for a human to examine first. In regions with few specialists it could bring expert diagnosis to patients who would otherwise wait months.

      D Reading images is only one application. A different kind of program has transformed a problem that had defeated biologists for fifty years: predicting the three-dimensional shape of a protein from its chemical sequence. The shape determines what a protein does in the body, and working it out in the laboratory could take years. In 2020 a system called AlphaFold showed that it could predict shapes almost as accurately as experiments, and its makers have since published predictions for some 200 million proteins. Researchers designing new medicines now routinely begin with these.

      E Less glamorous uses may matter just as much. Doctors in many countries spend as much time on paperwork as with patients. Programs that listen to a consultation and produce a written summary, or that draft letters and fill in forms, could give some of that time back. Such tools must be checked carefully, however, because language programs occasionally state invented 'facts' with complete confidence.

      F Experience has also shown that success in the laboratory does not guarantee success in the clinic. A program for detecting eye disease in people with diabetes, which had been more than ninety per cent accurate in tests, was tried in several clinics in Thailand in 2020. There, photographs were often taken in poor light, and the system rejected more than a fifth of them as unusable; slow internet connections caused further delays. Nurses who had hoped to save time found themselves with extra work.

      G There are concerns as well. It is often impossible to explain exactly why a program reached a particular conclusion, which makes errors hard to detect. If a mistake harms a patient, it is unclear who is responsible: the hospital, the doctor or the company that built the software. For now, most health authorities insist that a qualified person must make the final decision.

      D The first modern attempt came in the 1990s. When the law was weakened, however, the company declared the car unprofitable, took the vehicles back and crushed nearly all of them in 2003, to the fury of their drivers.

      E The turning point is often dated to 2008, when a small Californian firm, Tesla, launched a sports car powered by several thousand of the lithium-ion cells used in laptop computers. It could travel almost 400 kilometres on one charge and accelerate faster than most petrol sports cars. It was expensive and sold in small numbers, but it destroyed the idea that an electric vehicle must be slow and dull, and the established manufacturers began to invest heavily in their own designs.

      F Part of the appeal lies in simplicity. A petrol engine and its gearbox contain around two thousand moving parts; an electric motor and its drive system have about twenty. There is no oil to change and far less to go wrong, so servicing costs less. Moreover, an electric car is only as clean as the electricity it uses: if that comes from coal-fired power stations, the benefit to the climate is much reduced.

      A Traditional manufacturing usually works by removing material: a block of metal or wood is cut, drilled and polished until the desired shape remains. Three-dimensional printing does the opposite. Guided by a digital design, a printer builds an object layer by layer, each one a fraction of a millimetre thick, from plastic, metal powder or other substances. For this reason engineers call the technique additive manufacturing.

      B The idea dates back to the 1980s, when it was used to make prototypes quickly. A company designing a new product could print a model overnight rather than waiting weeks for one to be made by hand. As the machines became cheaper and more precise, they began to produce finished goods as well.

      C The advantages are clearest where objects are complex or needed in small numbers. Aircraft manufacturers print lightweight engine parts with internal shapes that could not be made in any other way. In medicine the technology has been used for dental crowns, hearing aids and implants matched exactly to a patient's body. Because the printer uses only the material it needs, very little is wasted. Spare parts can be produced where they are required, even on the International Space Station, instead of being stored in warehouses and shipped around the world.

      D The spread of the technology beyond industry owes much to the expiry of a patent. Until 2009 the most common printing method was protected, and a machine cost tens of thousands of dollars. Once the patent ran out, small companies and enthusiasts began building simple printers that sold for a few hundred. Designs were shared freely online, and a worldwide community of amateur makers grew up. Their value was shown in 2020, when volunteers with home printers produced face shields for medical staff within days of supplies running short.

      E Builders have begun to print on a much larger scale. A robotic arm or a moving frame squeezes out a special quick-drying concrete, layer upon layer, rather as a baker pipes icing onto a cake. The walls of a small house can be completed in about twenty-four hours of printing, with far less waste than conventional building, and curved shapes cost no more than straight ones. Roofs, windows and wiring, however, still have to be added in the traditional way.

      F The most ambitious research aims to print living tissue. Instead of plastic, the printer deposits a gel containing human cells, which then grow together. Patches of skin and cartilage have been produced in this way and are used for testing medicines. Printing a complete organ such as a kidney remains a distant goal, mainly because nobody has yet found a way to reproduce the dense network of tiny blood vessels that every thick tissue needs in order to stay alive.

      G Three-dimensional printing is unlikely to replace factories, however. It remains slow compared with conventional methods, and for making millions of identical items, mass production is far cheaper. There are also worries about misuse, since designs for dangerous objects such as weapons can be shared online and printed at home.

      A The internet grew out of a research project funded by the United States Department of Defense in the 1960s. Its aim was to let scientists at different universities share expensive computers. The key idea was packet switching: instead of sending a message along one fixed line, as a telephone call was, the network broke it into small packets that travelled separately and were put back together at their destination. If one route failed, the packets simply took another.

      B The first link of the network, called ARPANET, was made in October 1969 between two universities in California. The operators tried to send the word 'login', but the system crashed after two letters, so the first message ever sent was 'lo'. By 1971 the network connected about twenty sites, and in the same year the engineer Ray Tomlinson sent the first email, choosing the @ sign to separate the user's name from the name of the computer.

      C During the 1970s other networks appeared, and they could not communicate with each other. Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn solved the problem by designing a common set of rules, known as TCP/IP, which ARPANET adopted on 1 January 1983. Many regard that date as the true birthday of the internet.

      D For ordinary people the turning point came later. In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at the CERN laboratory in Switzerland, proposed a system of linked pages that he named the World Wide Web. Crucially, CERN made the technology free for anyone to use. Within a decade the web had hundreds of millions of users, and the internet had moved from laboratories into homes.

      E The early web consisted mainly of plain text and was used chiefly by academics. That changed in 1993, when a team of students at the University of Illinois released Mosaic, a browser that displayed pictures on the same page as words and could be operated simply by pointing and clicking. It was easy to install, and within eighteen months it had several million users. Businesses realised that the web could reach the general public, and the first online shops and newspapers soon followed.

      F As the number of pages multiplied, finding anything became the central difficulty. The first guides were lists compiled by hand, which could not keep pace. In 1998 two students at Stanford University, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, founded Google around a new principle. Their search engine ranked a page according to how many other pages linked to it, treating each link as a kind of vote. The results were so much more useful than those of rival services that the company's name became a verb.

      G The physical side of the internet is easily forgotten. Despite talk of 'the cloud', more than ninety-five per cent of the data passing between continents travels through cables laid on the ocean floor, each no thicker than a garden hose. And access is far from universal: about a third of the world's people, most of them in poorer countries, still do not use the internet at all.

      A A drone is an aircraft without a pilot on board, flown either by remote control or by its own computer. Drones were developed for military purposes, but small, cheap models with four or more propellers and a camera have found a remarkable range of peaceful uses since about 2010.

      B Farmers were among the first to benefit. A drone flying over a field can photograph crops in different kinds of light, revealing areas that need water or are affected by disease long before the damage is visible from the ground. Fertiliser can then be applied only where it is required, saving money and reducing pollution. In Japan, unmanned helicopters have sprayed rice fields for decades.

      C Drones are also valuable where work is dangerous or access is difficult. They inspect bridges, power lines and wind turbines, jobs that used to require people to climb to great heights. After earthquakes and floods they search for survivors and map the damage. In Rwanda, a delivery service launched in 2016 flies blood and medicines to remote clinics, cutting journeys that took hours by road to about thirty minutes.

      D Conservation is another field that has been transformed. Counting animals from a light aircraft is expensive and risky; a drone can photograph a colony of seabirds or a herd of elephants without disturbing them, and computer software then counts the individuals. In African reserves, drones fitted with heat-sensitive cameras patrol at night and can pick out poachers from a distance. Some organisations are even using them to restore forests, firing capsules that contain seeds and nutrients into the ground far faster than people could plant by hand.

      E The entertainment industry has embraced the technology too. Sweeping shots from the air, which once required a helicopter and a large budget, are now within reach of any film-maker. And in a growing number of cities, displays in which hundreds or thousands of illuminated drones form moving pictures in the night sky are replacing fireworks, since they are quieter, can be reused and produce no smoke.

      F All of this depends on a machine that is remarkably simple to operate. A typical small drone stays level by itself: sensors measure its tilt hundreds of times a second and a tiny computer adjusts the speed of each propeller. Satellite positioning lets it hover over one spot or return automatically to its starting point if the signal from the controller is lost. The chief limitation is the battery. Most small models can remain in the air for only about half an hour.

      G The rapid spread of drones has raised problems. They can be flown over private gardens with a camera, and their noise disturbs both people and wildlife. More seriously, drones near airports have forced flights to be suspended. Most countries now require operators to register larger models, keep them within sight and stay away from crowds and runways. Whether city skies will ever be filled with drones delivering parcels, as some companies predict, depends as much on such rules as on technology.

      A Most smartphone users take it for granted that a blue dot on a map will show their position to within a few metres. Behind that dot is the Global Positioning System, a network of about thirty satellites orbiting roughly 20,000 kilometres above the Earth. The system was built by the United States military and became fully operational in 1995.

      B The principle is surprisingly simple. Each satellite continuously broadcasts a signal stating its position and the exact time. A receiver on the ground notes how long each signal took to arrive and, since radio waves travel at the speed of light, converts that delay into a distance. One satellite places the receiver somewhere on a huge sphere; with signals from four satellites, only a single point fits all the measurements.

      C Everything depends on timing. An error of one millionth of a second would put the position out by about 300 metres, so every satellite carries atomic clocks. Even Einstein's theory of relativity must be taken into account: because the satellites move fast and experience weaker gravity, their clocks run faster than clocks on the ground by about 38 millionths of a second per day. Without correction, the system would drift by around ten kilometres daily.

      D Originally the best signal was reserved for the military, and civilian receivers were deliberately made less accurate. That restriction ended in 2000, and accuracy improved overnight from about 100 metres to about ten. Today GPS and similar systems run by Europe, Russia and China guide aircraft, ships and tractors, and the precise time signals are used to coordinate mobile phone networks and banking transactions.

      E Satellite positioning has uses that its designers never imagined. Fixed receivers anchored to rock can detect movements of a few millimetres a year, allowing geologists to watch continents drift and to measure the strain building up along the faults where earthquakes occur. Biologists attach miniature receivers to animals from albatrosses to whales in order to follow their migrations. And because signals are slowed slightly by moisture in the air, weather services analyse the delays to improve their forecasts.

      F Yet the system is more fragile than most users realise. The signals arriving from space are extraordinarily faint, comparable to the light of a household bulb seen from 20,000 kilometres away, and they can be drowned out by a transmitter that costs very little. Such jammers are illegal in most countries, but they are used, for example by lorry drivers who do not want their employers to track them. More worrying still is the broadcasting of false signals, which can make a ship's instruments show a position many kilometres from the truth.

      G There may also be a cost to our own abilities. In experiments, people who followed spoken directions from a device remembered far less about a route than those who used a paper map, and brain scans indicate that the regions involved in finding one's way are less active when a machine does the work. Rescue teams tell of drivers who obeyed their instructions so faithfully that they ended up on mountain tracks, or in rivers.

      A Every hour, the Earth receives more energy from the Sun than humanity uses in a year. Capturing even a small part of it has long been a dream of engineers. The photovoltaic effect, in which light striking certain materials produces an electric current, was first observed by the French physicist Edmond Becquerel in 1839, but the first practical silicon solar cell was not made until 1954, at Bell Laboratories in the United States.

      B That early cell converted only about six per cent of the light into electricity and was extremely expensive. Its first important customers were space agencies, which needed a lightweight source of power for satellites and were not worried about cost. On Earth, solar panels were for decades limited to small devices such as calculators and to remote places far from power lines.

      C The picture has changed dramatically. Typical panels today have an efficiency of around twenty per cent, and mass production, much of it in China, has reduced their price by about ninety per cent since 2010. In many sunny countries solar farms are now the cheapest way of generating new electricity. Panels have no moving parts, make no noise and can last for twenty-five years or more.

      D The obvious drawback is that the Sun does not always shine. Output falls on cloudy days and stops at night, often just when demand rises in the evening. The solution lies in storage. Large batteries are being installed beside solar farms, and some power stations pump water uphill during the day and release it through turbines after dark. Until storage becomes cheaper, most countries will continue to need other sources alongside solar.

      E Photovoltaic panels are not the only way of using sunlight. In a concentrated solar power station, thousands of mirrors turn to follow the Sun and reflect its rays onto a receiver at the top of a tower. The intense heat is absorbed by molten salt, which can be kept hot in insulated tanks for many hours and used to make steam for turbines whenever electricity is required. A large plant of this type on the edge of the Sahara in Morocco continues to supply power for several hours after sunset.

      F Solar energy is having perhaps its greatest effect in places that have never been connected to a power grid. Hundreds of millions of people, most of them in rural Africa and South Asia, still light their homes with kerosene lamps, which are expensive to run, give poor light and fill rooms with harmful smoke. A small panel on the roof, with a battery, can power several lamps, charge a mobile phone and run a radio. Many families buy such kits by paying small sums each week through their phones.

      G Large solar farms require a great deal of space, and this has led to some inventive solutions. Panels are being floated on reservoirs, where they also reduce the loss of water through evaporation, and raised above fields so that crops can grow or sheep can graze in the partial shade beneath them. A problem for the future is disposal. The first generation of panels is now wearing out, and the industry has only begun to develop ways of recovering the glass, silicon and silver they contain.

      A The word 'robot' comes from a Czech play of 1920, in which artificial workers rebel against their human masters. Real robots arrived forty years later and were far less dramatic. In 1961 a machine called Unimate, essentially a mechanical arm, began lifting hot pieces of metal at a General Motors car plant in New Jersey, a job that was unpleasant and dangerous for people.

      B Industrial robots spread through car factories in the 1970s and 1980s, particularly in Japan. They were ideal for tasks such as welding and painting, which had to be repeated thousands of times in exactly the same way. A robot does not get bored, take breaks or lose concentration. On the other hand, the early machines were blind and inflexible. They had to be fenced off in cages, because they could not sense a person standing in their path.

      C A newer generation, known as collaborative robots or 'cobots', is designed to work beside people. Equipped with cameras and sensors, they stop immediately when they touch something unexpected, and they can be taught a new task simply by guiding the arm through the movements. Because they are relatively cheap, even small firms can afford them.

      D Outside the factory, the largest numbers of robots are now found in warehouses. In the huge distribution centres of online retailers, low wheeled machines slide beneath shelving units, lift them and carry them to a human worker, who picks out the item that a customer has ordered. The worker stays in one place, and the shelves come to her. The arrangement illustrates a division of labour that is typical of the present stage of automation: machines do the carrying, while people do whatever requires a skilful hand.

      E The reason is a puzzle first noted by the robotics researcher Hans Moravec in the 1980s. Tasks that people find difficult, such as playing chess or multiplying large numbers, are comparatively easy for a computer. Things that a small child does without thinking, such as picking up an unfamiliar object, folding a towel or walking over rough ground, turn out to be extraordinarily hard. A robot that can pick ripe strawberries without bruising them at anything like the speed of a human worker has still to be perfected.

      F This helps to explain why the household robot promised by science fiction has failed to arrive. The one machine that has entered homes in large numbers is the robotic vacuum cleaner, tens of millions of which have been sold since 2002; it succeeds because floors are flat and the task is simple. A general-purpose domestic helper, able to tidy a room or load a dishwasher, would have to cope with an environment far less predictable than any factory.

      G Whether robots destroy jobs is a matter of debate. Studies in several countries have found that each new industrial robot replaces a number of factory workers. Yet countries with the highest numbers of robots, such as South Korea and Germany, do not have unusually high unemployment. Economists point out that automation also creates work, in programming, maintenance and new industries, although those jobs demand different skills, and workers who lose routine jobs often find it hard to move into them.

      A The average smartphone owner now checks the device dozens of times a day, often without any particular purpose. This is not an accident. Many of the most popular apps are free to use, and the companies behind them earn money by selling advertising. The longer people stay on the screen, the more advertisements they see. Human attention has become the product being sold.

      B Designers have a range of techniques for holding that attention. One is the endless feed: because there is no natural stopping point, such as the end of a page, users keep scrolling. Another is the notification, a sound or red symbol that creates a small sense of urgency. A third is the unpredictable reward. Psychologists have known since the 1950s that animals repeat an action most persistently when it is rewarded only some of the time. Refreshing a social media page works in a similar way: usually there is nothing new, but occasionally there is a message or a 'like'.

      C The consequences are disputed. Some researchers link heavy use of social media to anxiety and poor sleep among teenagers, while others argue that the evidence is weak and that the effects are small. What is less controversial is the cost to concentration. In one experiment, students performed worse on a test when their phone was simply lying on the desk, even though it was switched off.

      D The business of selling attention is older than the internet. In 1833 a young New York printer, Benjamin Day, launched a newspaper called the Sun at a price of one cent, when its rivals cost six. He sold it for less than it cost to produce and made his profit from advertisers, who paid to reach his large readership. To attract readers he filled the paper with crime stories and sensational reports, including a famous series claiming that life had been discovered on the Moon. Radio and television later adopted the same model.

      E What is new is the precision and persistence of the modern version, and its effect on how people work. Many users believe they can attend to several things at once. Research at Stanford University found the opposite: people who habitually juggled several streams of media performed worse than others on tests of concentration, and, surprisingly, were also slower at switching from one task to another. Other studies of office workers suggest that after an interruption it takes many minutes to return fully to the original task.

      F Some of the people who built these systems have come to regret them. The designer who invented the endless feed has said publicly that he had not foreseen how much time it would consume and now campaigns for more humane technology. A former executive of a large social network has admitted that its features were deliberately engineered to exploit a weakness in human psychology.

      G In response, phone makers have introduced tools that show how much time is spent on each app and allow users to set limits. Critics note the irony of relying on the device itself to solve the problem, and suggest a simpler remedy: leaving it in another room.

      A Plastic is one of the most useful materials ever invented: light, strong, waterproof and cheap. These same qualities make it a problem once it is thrown away. Since large-scale production began in the 1950s, more than eight billion tonnes have been manufactured, and it is estimated that less than ten per cent of all plastic waste has ever been recycled. The rest has been burned, buried or left in the environment.

      B One reason is that 'plastic' is not a single substance. There are many types, and they cannot be melted down together. A drinks bottle is made of one kind, its cap of another, and the label of a third. Waste must therefore be sorted, which is costly, and food remains can spoil a whole batch. Even when recycling succeeds, the quality of the material declines each time, so a bottle is more likely to become carpet fibre than another bottle.

      C For years many rich countries dealt with the difficulty by shipping their plastic waste abroad, chiefly to China. In 2018 China banned most of these imports, and waste began to pile up in the exporting countries or was diverted to nations with weaker controls.

      D One proposed alternative is plastic made from plants such as maize or sugar cane rather than from oil. These 'bioplastics' sound attractive, but the label can mislead. Many of them break down only in industrial composting plants, where the temperature is kept at around sixty degrees; in a garden heap or in the sea they last almost as long as ordinary plastic. If they are mixed with conventional plastic waste, moreover, they can spoil the recycled material.

      E A more surprising possibility emerged in 2016, when Japanese scientists examining samples from a bottle-recycling site discovered a bacterium that had evolved the ability to feed on the plastic used for drinks bottles. The enzymes it produces cut the long molecules into their original components. Researchers in several countries have since modified these enzymes to work many times faster, and a French company is building a plant that will use them to turn old bottles and polyester clothing into new plastic.

      F Governments, meanwhile, have turned to the law. Rwanda prohibited plastic bags as early as 2008 and searches travellers' luggage for them at the border. The European Union banned a list of throwaway items, including plastic straws, cutlery and cotton buds, in 2021. Even modest measures can be effective: after large shops in England were required to charge a small sum for each carrier bag, the number handed out by the main supermarkets fell by more than ninety per cent.

      G Several solutions are being explored. Chemical recycling breaks plastic down into its original building blocks, which can be made into new material of full quality, though the process uses a great deal of energy. Deposit schemes, in which customers get money back for returning bottles, achieve return rates above ninety per cent in countries such as Germany and Norway. Most experts stress, however, that the priority must be to use less plastic in the first place.

      A By 2050 about two thirds of the world's population is expected to live in cities, far from the fields that feed them. One response has been to bring agriculture into the city itself. Urban farming takes many forms, from community gardens on empty plots to greenhouses on supermarket roofs.

      B The most ambitious version is the vertical farm. Inside a warehouse or a disused factory, lettuces and herbs grow on shelves stacked many levels high. There is no soil: the roots sit in water containing nutrients, a method known as hydroponics, and LED lamps replace the sun. Because the environment is sealed, no pesticides are needed, and the crop is unaffected by drought, frost or storms. Such farms use up to ninety-five per cent less water than open fields, and harvests continue all year round.

      C There are further benefits. Food grown where it is eaten does not need to be transported long distances, so it arrives fresher. Community gardens also bring neighbours together and give children who have grown up among concrete a chance to learn where food comes from.

      D Growing food in cities is not a new idea. During the Second World War, governments urged citizens to dig up lawns and parks, and in the United States some twenty million 'victory gardens' are estimated to have supplied about forty per cent of the country's vegetables. A more recent example is Havana. When the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 cut off Cuba's supplies of fuel and fertiliser, the city's inhabitants turned empty plots into organic gardens, which still provide a large share of the fresh vegetables eaten in the capital.

      E Today the most determined efforts are being made where land is scarcest. Singapore, a crowded island state that imports about ninety per cent of its food, has set a target of producing thirty per cent of its nutritional needs at home by 2030. Farms have appeared on the roofs of multi-storey car parks and housing blocks, and the government offers grants to companies developing new techniques.

      F One such technique combines plants with fish. In an aquaponic system, fish are raised in tanks and the water, rich in their waste, is pumped through beds of vegetables. Bacteria convert the waste into nutrients that the plants absorb, and the cleaned water returns to the fish. The result is two crops from the same water, with almost nothing discharged. The method is not simple, however, since the needs of fish, plants and bacteria must be kept in careful balance.

      G Critics are not convinced that vertical farms can feed cities. The lamps and climate control consume a great deal of electricity, and several well-funded companies have gone bankrupt because of energy costs. Moreover, the crops that grow well indoors are leafy vegetables, which supply few calories. Wheat, rice and maize, the staple foods of humanity, need far too much space and light to be grown this way at a reasonable price. Urban farms may add welcome freshness to city diets, but the countryside will remain essential.

      C The consequences reach far beyond the forest itself. Tropical forests contain more than half of the world's land species, many of which live nowhere else. Trees also store vast amounts of carbon, and when they are burned or left to rot it is released as carbon dioxide; deforestation accounts for roughly a tenth of global emissions. Forests even make their own weather. Trees draw water from the ground and release it through their leaves, and this moisture falls again as rain. Scientists fear that if too much of the Amazon is cut, the remainder could dry out and turn into grassland.

      D It may seem strange that land which supports such luxuriant vegetation makes poor farmland, but the soil beneath most tropical forests is thin and infertile. Almost all the nutrients are held in the living plants themselves. When a leaf falls, it decays within weeks in the warm, damp conditions, and the minerals are taken up again at once by roots near the surface. Once the trees are cut and burned, heavy rain washes the remaining goodness away, and after a few harvests the farmer must often clear a fresh patch.

      E Damage is not confined to the areas that are actually cleared. As roads and fields advance, the forest is broken into isolated fragments. Wind and sunlight penetrate the exposed edges, drying the vegetation and making it vulnerable to fire, which in an undisturbed rainforest is almost unknown. Large animals such as jaguars, which need extensive territories, disappear from small fragments first, and the trees whose seeds they spread follow.

      F A popular response has been to plant trees, and governments and companies have announced schemes to plant billions. Scientists caution that such projects are no substitute for protecting what already exists. Many consist of a single fast-growing species, such as eucalyptus, grown in rows for timber; these plantations shelter few animals and hold far less carbon than an old forest. Where conditions allow, simply fencing off damaged land and letting the forest return naturally is often cheaper and more effective.

      G There are some encouraging signs. Satellite monitoring now allows illegal clearing to be spotted within days. Costa Rica, which pays landowners to protect trees, has doubled its forest cover since the 1980s. Consumers have a role too, since several large companies have promised, under public pressure, to buy only products that are not linked to deforestation.

      A Every year an estimated eight to eleven million tonnes of plastic enter the sea, roughly a lorry load every minute. About eighty per cent of it comes from the land, carried by rivers or blown from beaches and rubbish dumps. The rest is lost or thrown overboard at sea, and abandoned fishing nets make up a large part of this.

      B Ocean currents gather floating debris into huge rotating zones. The best known, the Great Pacific Garbage Patch between Hawaii and California, is often imagined as an island of rubbish, but this is misleading. Most of it is a thin soup of small fragments, hardly visible from a boat.

      C Plastic does not decay as natural materials do. Sunlight and waves merely break it into smaller and smaller pieces. Fragments under five millimetres across are called microplastics, and they have now been found everywhere from Arctic ice to the deepest ocean trench. They also come from sources that few people suspect, such as the fibres washed out of synthetic clothes and the dust from car tyres.

      D The harm to wildlife is well documented. Turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, and seabirds feed bottle tops to their chicks, which may starve with full stomachs. Animals become entangled in old nets and drown. Microplastics are swallowed by tiny creatures at the bottom of the food chain and pass upwards to fish and eventually to humans, though the effect on our health is not yet known.

      E Lost fishing gear is especially destructive. A net made of nylon does not rot, and after it has been abandoned it may drift for years, still trapping fish, turtles and seals, a process known as ghost fishing. When researchers analysed the contents of the Pacific patch in 2018, they found that nets accounted for almost half of its total weight. Some fishing communities now mark their gear so that lost nets can be traced, and pay crews to bring old ones back to port.

      F Rivers are the main route by which plastic from the land reaches the sea. It was once thought that a handful of great rivers carried most of it, but more detailed studies point instead to about a thousand smaller ones, typically short rivers flowing through crowded coastal cities in Asia, where heavy rain washes uncollected rubbish straight into the water. This finding is in one sense encouraging, since a river is a far easier place to intercept waste than the open sea. Floating barriers that guide debris to a collection point are already operating in several cities.

      G Records kept by volunteers who clean beaches give a useful picture of what is being thrown away. Year after year, the commonest items are much the same: cigarette ends, food wrappers, bottles and their caps, bags and straws. Almost all are objects designed to be used once, for a few minutes, and then discarded.

      H Cleaning the open ocean is extremely difficult, so most specialists believe efforts should focus on stopping plastic at its source, by improving waste collection in coastal cities and reducing throwaway packaging.

      A Seen from space, the Earth looks like a planet with water to spare. In fact about ninety-seven per cent of that water is salty. Of the remaining fresh water, more than two thirds is frozen in glaciers and ice caps, and most of the rest lies underground. Rivers and lakes, on which humanity mainly depends, hold a tiny fraction of one per cent of the total.

      B Demand on this limited supply has grown about six times over the past century. Contrary to what many people assume, households are not the main consumers. Agriculture takes roughly seventy per cent of all the fresh water that people use, industry around twenty per cent and homes only about ten. Some crops are particularly thirsty: producing a single kilogram of rice can require more than two thousand litres.

      C The results are visible in many regions. Great rivers such as the Colorado and the Yellow River sometimes fail to reach the sea. Underground reserves in northern India and the central United States are being pumped out much faster than rain can refill them. Around two billion people live in countries where water is under severe pressure, and climate change is making rainfall less reliable.

      D A great deal of water is consumed invisibly, in the things we buy. Producing a single cotton T-shirt requires roughly 2,700 litres, a cup of coffee about 140 litres and a kilogram of beef as much as 15,000 litres, most of it used to grow the animals' feed. Economists call this 'virtual water'. When a dry country imports grain or meat instead of producing it, it is in effect importing the water that was needed to grow it, and this trade allows many nations in arid regions to feed far more people than their own rivers could support.

      E Because most great rivers flow through several countries, it is often predicted that the wars of the future will be fought over water. Tension certainly exists: Egypt, which depends almost entirely on the Nile, has protested strongly against a huge dam built upstream by Ethiopia. History, however, offers some reassurance. Researchers who examined relations between states sharing rivers over half a century found that agreements were far more common than violence. A treaty dividing the waters of the Indus between India and Pakistan, signed in 1960, has survived several wars between the two.

      F Cities, too, can run short. In early 2018, after three years of drought, the South African city of Cape Town announced that within weeks it would have to turn off the taps in most homes, a moment officials named 'Day Zero'. Residents were limited to fifty litres a person per day, less than a short shower and a few flushes of a toilet require. The city's consumption fell to roughly half its previous level, the rains returned that winter, and Day Zero never arrived.

      G Solutions exist, but none is simple. Drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of plants, can cut a farm's use by half compared with flooding fields. Cities lose a great deal through leaking pipes, in some cases a third or more of their supply. Removing salt from seawater is technically possible but remains expensive. Many economists argue that water is wasted mainly because it is priced too low, although raising the price of something so essential is politically difficult.

      A People have used the wind for thousands of years, to drive sailing ships and to turn mills that ground grain and pumped water. Using it to make electricity began in the late nineteenth century, but wind power became a serious industry only after the oil crisis of the 1970s, when Denmark in particular began investing in it.

      B A modern turbine is a huge machine. Its tower may be over a hundred metres tall, and each of its three blades can be longer than the wing of a large passenger aircraft. Size matters, because doubling the length of the blades roughly quadruples the energy captured, and winds are stronger and steadier higher up. A single large turbine can supply electricity for several thousand homes.

      C Increasingly, turbines are being built out at sea. Offshore winds are more powerful and more constant than those on land, and there are no neighbours to complain about noise or spoiled views. The disadvantage is cost: foundations must be fixed to the seabed, and salt water makes maintenance difficult. The newest designs float, anchored by cables, so that they can be placed in deep water.

      D The pioneer of wind electricity was a Scottish engineer, James Blyth. In 1887 he built a turbine with cloth sails in the garden of his holiday cottage and used it to charge batteries that lit the house, the first in the world to be powered by the wind. He offered the surplus current to light the main street of the village, but the inhabitants declined, reportedly regarding electricity as the work of the devil. A few months later an American inventor, Charles Brush, constructed a far larger machine with 144 wooden blades beside his mansion in Ohio.

      E A modern turbine works on the same principle as an aircraft wing. Air flowing over the curved blades creates lift, which turns the rotor, and a generator in the housing at the top of the tower converts the motion into electricity. Sensors measure the direction of the wind, and motors turn the whole head to face it. Turbines begin to generate in a light breeze and reach full output in a strong one, but in a gale they are shut down automatically to avoid damage.

      F Public attitudes depend a good deal on who benefits. In Denmark many early turbines were bought by cooperatives of local residents, and by the early 2000s more than 100,000 families owned shares in one. People who receive an income from a turbine, it appears, are much less inclined to object to the sight of it. Where wind farms belong to distant companies, opposition from neighbours has often been fierce.

      G Wind power has drawbacks. Its output varies with the weather, so other sources or storage are needed for calm days. Turbines kill birds and bats, though studies indicate that the numbers are far smaller than those killed by cats or by collisions with buildings. Old blades, made of materials that are hard to recycle, often end up buried in the ground. Nevertheless, wind now provides more than half of Denmark's electricity, and its share is rising steadily worldwide.
