      A When Yellowstone became the world's first national park in 1872, wolves were regarded as dangerous pests. Hunters, encouraged by the government, shot or poisoned them, and by 1926 the last pack in the park had been killed.

      B The effects appeared slowly. Without their main predator, the elk, a large species of deer, multiplied. They no longer needed to keep moving, and they gathered along river banks, where they ate young willow and aspen trees down to the ground. As the trees vanished, so did the songbirds that nested in them. Beavers, which need willow for food and for building their dams, became rare, and the ponds that their dams had created dried up.

      C In 1995, after years of argument, biologists brought fourteen wolves from Canada and released them in the park; seventeen more followed the next year. The wolves killed some elk, but, equally important, they changed the behaviour of the rest. Elk began to avoid valleys where they could easily be trapped. In those places the trees recovered, and beavers and birds returned. The wolves also reduced the number of coyotes, so that the small animals coyotes hunt increased, providing more food for foxes and eagles.

      D Some researchers have gone further and claimed that the wolves altered the rivers themselves. As willows and other plants returned to the banks, the argument runs, their roots held the soil together, so that the channels became narrower and deeper and wandered less. The new beaver dams slowed the current and created pools in which fish and frogs could breed. A short film presenting this story has been watched online tens of millions of times.

      E Yellowstone is not the only place where the removal of a predator has had unexpected results. Along the Pacific coast of North America, sea otters were hunted almost to extinction for their fur by the early twentieth century. Otters eat sea urchins, spiny animals that feed on the giant seaweed known as kelp. With the otters gone, urchins multiplied and chewed through the stems of the kelp, turning underwater forests full of fish into bare rock. Where otters have since been protected and have returned, the kelp has grown back.

      F In Europe, wolves are coming back without human help. Protected by law since the 1980s, they have spread from the east and south into countries where they had been absent for a century or more; the first pack in modern Germany was recorded in 2000, and there are now well over a hundred. The animals have shown that they can live surprisingly close to people, but attacks on sheep have made their return controversial, and governments pay for electric fences and guard dogs.

      G The story has become a famous example of what ecologists call a trophic cascade, in which a change at the top of the food chain flows down through every level. Some scientists warn that it has been simplified: milder winters, drought and hunting outside the park also affected the elk. Even so, few now doubt that large predators shape the landscapes they live in. Farmers near the park, whose sheep and cattle are sometimes attacked, remain less enthusiastic.

      A A glacier is a mass of ice that forms on land where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Over many years the snow is compressed into dense ice, and when it becomes thick enough it begins to move downhill under its own weight, usually by less than a metre a day. Glaciers and the great ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica hold about seventy per cent of the world's fresh water.

      B Glaciers are powerful sculptors. During the ice ages they carved the deep U-shaped valleys of the Alps and the fjords of Norway, and they left behind the basins that became the Great Lakes of North America.

      C Today almost all of the world's glaciers are retreating. Photographs taken a century apart show valleys once filled with ice now occupied by bare rock and lakes. The Alps have lost roughly half of their ice volume since 1900, and some small glaciers have disappeared completely. The cause is rising temperature: a glacier is highly sensitive to climate because a change of only a degree or so tips the balance between snowfall and melting.

      D The retreating ice is giving up objects that it has held for thousands of years. The most celebrated discovery was made in 1991, when two hikers in the Alps on the border between Austria and Italy noticed a body protruding from the ice. They assumed it was an unlucky climber, but it proved to be a man who had died about 5,300 years ago. With him were a copper axe, a bow, arrows and clothing of leather and woven grass, all remarkably preserved. In Norway, melting ice patches have yielded ancient skis, arrows and even a woollen tunic.

      E Melting also creates a serious hazard. As a glacier shrinks, water collects in a lake behind the bank of loose rock that the ice has left at its lower end. Such natural dams are unstable. If one gives way, perhaps after an avalanche falls into the lake, millions of cubic metres of water are released in minutes. In 1941 a flood of this kind destroyed a large part of the Peruvian city of Huaraz and killed several thousand people. Engineers in Peru, Nepal and Bhutan now lower the level of the most dangerous lakes by digging channels or tunnels.

      F Some communities have tried to slow the melting directly. Each summer, workers in Switzerland cover part of the Rhone Glacier with white blankets, which reflect sunlight and have been shown to cut the loss of ice beneath them by more than half. The measure protects an ice cave visited by tourists, but nobody pretends that it could save a whole glacier: the cost would be enormous.

      G The loss matters to people far from the mountains. Glaciers act as natural reservoirs, storing water in winter and releasing it in the dry summer months when rivers would otherwise run low. Hundreds of millions of people in South and Central Asia depend on rivers fed by the ice of the Himalayas and neighbouring ranges, including the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya. As glaciers shrink, river flow first increases, sometimes causing floods, and then declines permanently. Melting land ice also adds to the rise in sea level, which threatens low-lying coasts and islands.

      A Noise is perhaps the most underestimated form of pollution. It leaves no visible trace and disappears the moment its source is switched off, so it is easy to dismiss as a mere annoyance. Evidence gathered over the past few decades suggests it is considerably more than that.

      B Sound is measured in decibels. Normal conversation is about 60 decibels, heavy traffic around 85 and a rock concert well over 100. Long exposure to levels above 85 decibels can permanently damage hearing. But harm occurs at much lower levels too. The body reacts to noise as a signal of danger, releasing stress hormones and raising blood pressure, and it continues to do so during sleep, even when the sleeper does not wake. Large studies in Europe have found that people living beside busy roads or under flight paths have a higher risk of heart disease.

      C Children seem to be especially vulnerable. In a well-known study in New York in the 1970s, pupils in classrooms facing a railway line were found to be almost a year behind in reading compared with those on the quiet side of the same building. When the noise was reduced, the gap disappeared.

      D Wildlife suffers as well. Birds in cities sing at a higher pitch or at night in order to be heard, and the engines of ships interfere with the calls that whales use to communicate over great distances.

      E Complaints about noise are nothing new. In 1906 a New York doctor's wife, Julia Barnett Rice, founded a society to campaign against what she called unnecessary noise, beginning with the tugboats that sounded their whistles all night on the river beside her home. She collected evidence that the din was harming patients in the city's hospitals, and her efforts led to the first quiet zones around hospitals and schools, an idea soon copied elsewhere.

      F True quiet has since become rare. Teachers once treated this habit, known as code-switching, as a sign of laziness or of imperfect knowledge. Linguists who have analysed recordings disagree.       A To an adult, a child building a tower of blocks or pretending to be a pirate may appear to be doing nothing useful. Developmental psychologists see things differently. Play, they argue, is the main way in which young children learn about the world and about one another.

      B Different kinds of play develop different abilities. Physical play, such as running, climbing and wrestling, builds strength and coordination and teaches children to judge risk. Building with blocks or sand introduces ideas of size, balance and number. Most important of all, perhaps, is pretend play. When children agree that a cardboard box is a spaceship, they must negotiate roles, follow shared rules and control their impulses. A child who is playing a guard, for example, will stand still far longer than one who is simply told to do so.

      C The Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky observed in the 1930s that in play a child behaves 'a head taller than himself', practising skills that are still slightly beyond him. More recent research supports this. Children who have plenty of opportunity for free play tend to be better at solving problems and at getting along with others.

      D Human children are not the only young that play. Kittens stalk and pounce, young goats leap and puppies wrestle, and biologists have long asked why animals should spend energy on activities that can attract predators. Experiments with rats give part of the answer. Young rats prevented from play-fighting with others grow into adults that cannot read social signals properly: faced with a stranger, they either panic or attack without cause. Play, it seems, is how a young mammal's brain learns to deal with the unexpected.

      E An influential idea about children's play came from Denmark. In the 1930s the landscape architect Carl Theodor Sorensen noticed that children ignored the tidy playgrounds he had designed and preferred to play on building sites. In 1943 he opened a 'junk playground' in a suburb of Copenhagen, supplied with planks, bricks, old tyres and tools, where children could build and demolish as they pleased under the eye of a single adult. The idea spread to many countries after the war under the name of adventure playground.

      F Since then playgrounds in much of the world have moved in the opposite direction, with soft rubber surfaces and low equipment designed above all to prevent injury. Some researchers think this has gone too far. The Norwegian psychologist Ellen Sandseter argues that children have a natural appetite for mild risk, such as climbing high or moving fast, and that by mastering it they gradually overcome their fears. A child who is never allowed to feel slightly afraid, she suggests, may grow up more fearful, not less.

      G Despite this, time for play has been shrinking. In many countries formal lessons in reading and arithmetic begin earlier than they used to, school breaks have been shortened, and parents worried about traffic and strangers are less willing to let children play outside alone. Some experts connect these changes with rising levels of anxiety among young people. They point to Finland, where children do not start formal schooling until the age of seven, yet achieve excellent results later on.

      B What does the research show? The most thorough reviews have been carried out by the psychologist Harris Cooper, who analysed dozens of studies. He found that for secondary school students, those who did homework achieved better test results, up to a point: beyond about two hours a night, the benefit disappeared. For primary school children, however, there was almost no link between homework and achievement.

      C Comparisons between countries make the picture no clearer. Surveys of fifteen-year-olds carried out for the OECD, an international economic organisation, found that pupils in Shanghai spent about fourteen hours a week on homework, while those in Finland and South Korea spent less than three. Within a single country, schools that set more homework do tend to achieve better results, but across countries the amount appears to explain very little.

      D How pupils work may be more important than how long. Researchers in Spain who studied more than 7,000 teenagers found that those who did their homework regularly and without help did better in mathematics and science tests than those who spent longer on it or who relied on their parents. About an hour a day seemed to be the most effective amount; beyond that, results did not improve. Well-meant assistance from parents can even be harmful if it removes the need for the child to think.

      E Some authorities have tried to abolish homework by law. In France, written homework for primary school children has officially been forbidden since 1956, on the grounds that it increases inequality, but teachers have continued to set it and most parents expect it. Several American primary schools have recently replaced all homework with a simple request that pupils read a book of their own choice each evening.

Opponents answer that it eats into time for play, sport, sleep and family life, and that it is unfair. A child with educated parents, a quiet room and a computer has a clear advantage over one who has none of these, so homework may widen the gap between rich and poor.

      G Many teachers have concluded that quality matters more than quantity. Short tasks that practise what was taught in class or that ask pupils to read for pleasure seem more valuable than long worksheets. Cooper himself recommends the 'ten-minute rule': ten minutes a night in the first year of school, increasing by ten minutes with each year.

      A Why do some people give up after a failure while others try harder? The American psychologist Carol Dweck has spent several decades studying this question. Her answer is that much depends on what people believe about their own abilities.

      B According to Dweck, individuals with a 'fixed mindset' see intelligence as something you are born with and cannot change. For them, every task is a test of how clever they are. Because failure would show that they lack ability, they tend to avoid challenges and lose interest when work becomes hard. Those with a 'growth mindset', by contrast, believe that ability can be developed through effort and good strategies. They treat mistakes as information and are more likely to persist.

      C In one famous experiment, children were given a set of puzzles and then praised. Some were told, 'You must be smart at this'; others, 'You must have worked hard.' When offered a choice afterwards, most of those praised for intelligence chose an easy task, whereas most of those praised for effort chose a more difficult one from which they could learn. After a later, very hard set of problems, the first group's performance fell, while the second group improved.

      D The effects of praise can be traced back to the first years of life. In a long-term American study, researchers filmed parents at home with their children aged between one and three and counted how often they praised effort ('you worked hard on that') as opposed to qualities ('you're so clever'). Five years later, the children who had heard a larger proportion of praise for effort were more likely to say that they enjoyed difficult tasks and to believe that people can become smarter.

      E Teachers have looked for practical ways of applying the idea. Dweck often describes a high school in Chicago where students who had not passed a course received the grade 'Not Yet' rather than a fail. The words, she argues, tell a student that he or she is on a path towards success and has simply not arrived. Other schools encourage pupils to add the word 'yet' to statements such as 'I can't do fractions', or display work in progress on the walls alongside finished pieces.

      F Sport supplies some of the favourite illustrations. The American basketball player Michael Jordan, often called the greatest in the history of the game, was not selected for the senior team at his high school at the age of fifteen. By his own account the disappointment drove him to practise for hours each morning before lessons. Stories of this kind are inspiring, though critics point out that they prove little, since nobody collects the stories of those who practised just as hard without becoming famous.

      G These ideas have been enthusiastically adopted by schools, sometimes too simply. Dweck has criticised the notion that teachers need only praise effort; effort that leads nowhere should prompt a change of method. Moreover, large studies testing mindset lessons have found that the improvement in grades is modest, and concentrated among pupils who were previously struggling. A growth mindset appears to be helpful, but it is not a magic solution.

Regular exercise lowers the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and several cancers. It strengthens bones, helps to control weight and improves sleep. The World Health Organization recommends that adults do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity, such as brisk walking, every week, yet about a quarter of the world's adults fail to reach this level.

      B The scientific study of the subject began in London in the late 1940s. A doctor named Jeremy Morris noticed that the drivers of the city's double-decker buses, who sat all day, had roughly twice as many heart attacks as the conductors, who climbed around 600 stairs during each shift collecting fares. Later he found a similar difference between office clerks and postmen who delivered letters on foot.

      C The effects on the mind are equally impressive. Exercise increases the flow of blood to the brain and stimulates the release of chemicals that improve mood. Several trials have found that for mild depression a programme of regular exercise can work about as well as medication. In older people it appears to slow the decline of memory.

      D A common belief is that exercise is mainly a way of burning calories. Research among the Hadza people of Tanzania, who still live by hunting and gathering, has complicated this view. Hadza men walk about eleven kilometres a day and women about six, yet when the anthropologist Herman Pontzer measured the energy they used, the daily totals were scarcely higher than those of office workers in Europe and America, once body size was allowed for. The body, it seems, adjusts to greater activity by spending less energy on other processes. This is why exercise alone seldom leads to much loss of weight, though it remains essential for almost every other aspect of health.

      E For people who claim they have no time, there is encouraging news. Researchers in Canada compared two groups of inactive men over twelve weeks. One group cycled at a steady pace for forty-five minutes three times a week. The other did sessions lasting only ten minutes, which included three bursts of all-out effort of twenty seconds each. At the end, the fitness of both groups had improved by almost the same amount.

      F Nor is it necessary to exercise every day. A large British study that followed more than 60,000 adults found that so-called weekend warriors, who packed all their activity into one or two days a week, had a risk of early death almost as low as that of people who spread the same amount over the week. What counts, apparently, is the total.

      G Importantly, the greatest gain comes from the first step. The difference in health between people who do nothing and those who do a little is much larger than the difference between moderate exercisers and athletes. Nor is a gym necessary. Gardening, dancing, cycling to work and taking the stairs all count. Researchers add a warning, however: an hour of exercise does not fully cancel out the harm of sitting still for the rest of the day.

      A For most of history sugar was a rare luxury. Honey and ripe fruit were the only sweet foods available to our ancestors, and scientists believe that the human liking for sweetness evolved because it signalled a safe and valuable source of energy. Cane sugar reached Europe in quantity only after plantations were established in the Caribbean in the seventeenth century, worked by enslaved Africans. Even in 1700 the average English person ate less than two kilograms a year.

      B Today consumption in many countries exceeds thirty kilograms per person. Much of it is hidden.       C One reason why the amount is hard to judge is that sugar appears on labels under more than fifty different names, among them dextrose, maltose, glucose syrup and fruit juice concentrate. Since ingredients are listed in order of weight, a manufacturer that uses three or four kinds can keep each of them lower down the list. Phrases such as 'no added sugar' can also mislead: a fruit smoothie may contain no sugar from a packet and yet deliver as much as a fizzy drink.

      D Why should sugar in juice matter if sugar in fruit does not? The answer lies in fibre. In a whole orange, the sugar is locked inside cells whose walls take time to digest, so it reaches the blood slowly. When the fruit is squeezed, the fibre is left behind and the sugar is absorbed almost at once. A sudden rise in blood sugar is followed by a surge of the hormone insulin and then a rapid fall, which leaves people tired and hungry again. It is also far easier to drink the juice of four oranges than to eat four oranges.

The first, saccharin, was discovered by accident in 1879 by a chemist who noticed a sweet taste on his fingers at dinner after a day in the laboratory. Reviewing the evidence in 2023, the World Health Organization concluded that sweeteners do not help people to control their weight in the long term and advised against relying on them.

      F The consequences for health are serious. Sugar is the main cause of tooth decay. Sugary drinks are particularly harmful because liquid calories do not make people feel full, so they are consumed on top of normal meals; high consumption is strongly linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes.       G Governments have begun to respond. More than fifty countries have introduced a tax on sugary drinks. In Britain a levy announced in 2016 led manufacturers to cut the sugar in many drinks before it even came into force. Critics object that such taxes fall most heavily on the poor, while supporters reply that the poor also suffer most from the diseases concerned.

      A Smallpox was one of the most feared diseases in history. It killed about three in ten of those it infected and left survivors scarred and sometimes blind. In eighteenth-century Europe it is thought to have caused 400,000 deaths every year.

      B People had long known that those who recovered never caught the disease again. In China, India and the Ottoman Empire this knowledge was used in a risky procedure: material from a smallpox sore was scratched into the skin of a healthy person, who usually developed a mild illness and was then protected. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, wife of the British ambassador in Constantinople, observed the practice and introduced it to England in 1721. It worked, but a small proportion of those treated died.

      C A safer method came from the English countryside. It was commonly said that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle, did not get smallpox. In 1796 the doctor Edward Jenner decided to test this. He took fluid from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes and scratched it into the arm of James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener. Six weeks later he exposed the boy to smallpox. James remained healthy. The new technique was named vaccination, from vacca, the Latin word for cow.

      D By modern standards the experiment was highly unethical, but its results spread around the world within a few years. In 1967 the World Health Organization launched a campaign to eliminate smallpox entirely. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 the disease was declared eradicated, the first, and so far the only, human disease to be wiped out.

      E The victory owed as much to strategy as to the vaccine. At first the plan was to vaccinate entire populations, a task that proved impossible in crowded and remote regions. In 1966 an American doctor working in Nigeria, William Foege, found himself with too little vaccine and tried a different approach. His team searched for every case of the disease and vaccinated only the people living around each patient, forming a protective ring that the virus could not cross. The method worked so well that it was adopted everywhere. Two inventions helped: a freeze-dried vaccine that survived for weeks in tropical heat, and a simple two-pronged needle that volunteers could learn to use in minutes.

      F The virus has not entirely vanished. Samples are officially kept in two high-security laboratories, one in the United States and one in Russia, and whether they should be destroyed has been argued over for decades. Those in favour of keeping them say they may be needed to develop new medicines; opponents point to the danger of an accident. The fear is not imaginary. In 1978, a year after the last natural case, a medical photographer in the English city of Birmingham died after the virus escaped from a research laboratory in the building where she worked.

      G The campaign's success inspired others. A global effort against polio, begun in 1988, has reduced the number of cases by more than ninety-nine per cent, although the disease has proved stubborn in a few areas affected by conflict.

      A In 1928 the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find that mould had grown on one of his laboratory dishes and that the bacteria around it had died. The substance responsible, penicillin, was turned into a usable drug during the Second World War, and it transformed medicine. Infections that had regularly killed people, from pneumonia to an infected scratch, became easily curable. Operations such as transplants, which leave patients open to infection, became possible.

      B Fleming himself was unable to extract the active substance in a stable form, and for ten years his discovery remained a laboratory curiosity. The work was taken up in 1939 by a team at Oxford University led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain. Their first human patient, in February 1941, was a policeman dying of an infection that had begun with a scratch. After a few injections he improved dramatically, but the supply was so small that the doctors had to recover the drug from his urine and use it again. When it finally ran out, he relapsed and died.

      C Britain at war could not spare factories, so Florey took the project to the United States. At a government laboratory in Illinois, researchers looked for a more productive strain of the mould and asked the public to send in samples. The best one turned up on a rotting melon bought at a local market. Combined with a new method of growing the mould in deep tanks, it raised production so sharply that by June 1944 there was enough penicillin to treat every wounded soldier in the Allied armies that landed in France.

      D Success set off a search for similar drugs, most of them produced by bacteria and fungi living in the soil. Streptomycin, discovered in 1943, was the first effective treatment for tuberculosis, and the next two decades are remembered as a golden age in which most of the main families of antibiotics were found.

      E Fleming himself predicted the problem that now threatens these gains. In his Nobel Prize lecture of 1945 he warned that using too little penicillin, or using it carelessly, would allow bacteria to become resistant. The mechanism is natural selection. In any large population of bacteria a few may by chance be able to survive a drug. When the others are killed, these survivors multiply, and bacteria can even pass resistance to different species.

      F Human behaviour has speeded up the process enormously. Antibiotics are frequently prescribed for colds and flu, which are caused by viruses and are unaffected by them. In some countries they can be bought without a prescription. Vast quantities are also given to healthy farm animals to make them grow faster. Resistant infections are already estimated to cause more than a million deaths a year worldwide.

      G Meanwhile, few new antibiotics are being developed. A drug that is taken for a week and deliberately used as little as possible earns much less than one taken daily for years, so pharmaceutical companies have little incentive. Proposed solutions include public funding for research, stricter rules on farm use, and rapid tests that tell a doctor whether an infection is bacterial at all.

The benefit continued to rise up to about 7,500 steps and then levelled off.

      D The advantages are not only physical. Experiments at Stanford University found that people produced far more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, which may explain why so many writers and thinkers, from Aristotle to Charles Darwin, were habitual walkers.       E Human beings are built for walking. Fossil footprints preserved in volcanic ash at Laetoli in Tanzania, discovered in 1978, show that our ancestors were walking upright on two legs at least 3.6 million years ago, long before their brains grew large.       F The speed at which an older person walks tells doctors a surprising amount. An analysis of nine studies covering some 34,000 people over sixty-five found that walking speed predicted how long they would live almost as accurately as detailed medical information. Some specialists now refer to it as an extra vital sign, to be measured like pulse and blood pressure.

      G Yet people in rich countries walk far less than they used to. In the United States, almost half of all children walked or cycled to school in 1969; forty years later the proportion had fallen to about one in eight. Longer distances are only part of the explanation. Parents interviewed in surveys mention fear of traffic above all, a danger that grows as more of them choose to drive.

      H Sadly, modern cities often discourage walking. Wide roads, long distances between homes and shops, and a lack of pavements make the car the only practical choice. Planners are now trying to design neighbourhoods in which daily needs lie within a fifteen-minute walk.

Recorded laughter was first added to an American comedy programme in 1950, and experiments have confirmed that audiences rate the same jokes as funnier when they hear other people laughing. Too many options, he argued, make deciding harder work, and after deciding we are less satisfied, because it is easy to imagine that one of the rejected alternatives would have been better. He distinguished two types of people. 'Maximisers' feel they must find the very best and compare endlessly, whereas 'satisficers' settle for something that is good enough.       D The effect was soon reported outside the supermarket. Iyengar examined the records of nearly 800,000 American employees who had been offered retirement savings plans by their companies. Where the plan contained only two investment funds, about three quarters of the staff joined. Where it offered fifty-nine, the proportion fell to about sixty per cent, even though by not joining people gave up money that their employer would have added to their savings.

      E Some companies have profited from the lesson. When a large manufacturer reduced its range of one brand of shampoo from twenty-six varieties to fifteen, sales of the brand rose by ten per cent. Customers have less to compare, shelves are easier to fill, and the savings are passed on in lower prices.

      F Making choices also seems to be tiring in itself. A study of more than a thousand decisions by judges considering whether to release prisoners early found that a prisoner's chances were best at the beginning of the day and immediately after a meal break, at about sixty-five per cent, and sank steadily to almost nothing just before the next break. When scientists combined the results of some fifty similar experiments, the average effect of having more choice was close to zero: sometimes it discouraged buyers and sometimes it did not. They were tired of shopkeepers who charged high prices for goods that were often adulterated; flour, for instance, was sometimes mixed with chalk. Their shop was different in one crucial respect: it belonged to its customers.

      B The rules they drew up, later known as the Rochdale Principles, became the foundation of the cooperative movement. Membership was open to all. Each member had one vote, regardless of how much money he or she had invested. Goods were to be pure and honestly weighed. Profits were returned to members in proportion to what they had bought, a payment called the dividend. A share of the surplus was set aside for education.

      C The model was copied widely. Today around a billion people worldwide are members of some kind of cooperative. Farmers join together to sell their milk or grain and to buy equipment. Credit unions offer savings and loans to their members. In worker cooperatives the employees themselves own the firm; the best known is Mondragon in the Basque region of Spain, a group of businesses with tens of thousands of worker-owners, where the highest-paid manager may earn only a few times more than the lowest-paid worker.

      D Some of the largest cooperatives are found in farming. In 1946 dairy farmers in the Indian state of Gujarat, tired of selling to a single private buyer at whatever price he offered, formed a cooperative to process and market their own milk. Under the brand name Amul it grew into an organisation owned by more than three million producers, many of whom keep only two or three animals. Its model was copied across the country, and India, once short of milk, became the world's largest producer.

      E In the United States, cooperatives brought electricity to the countryside. In the mid-1930s nine out of ten city homes had electric light, but only about one farm in ten, because private companies saw no profit in running lines to scattered customers. With the help of cheap government loans, farmers set up their own cooperatives to build the lines. Within fifteen years the great majority of farms were connected, and some nine hundred of these organisations still supply power today.

      F The cooperative principle is even applied in professional sport. FC Barcelona is not owned by a wealthy individual or a company but by well over a hundred thousand members, who pay a yearly fee and elect the club's president. In Germany a rule requires that members hold a majority of the votes in nearly every professional football club, which is one reason why ticket prices there have remained lower than in England.

      G Supporters argue that cooperatives are more stable than ordinary companies, since they are not under pressure from outside shareholders to maximise short-term profit, and studies indicate that they survive economic crises rather better. Their weakness is finance. Because they cannot sell shares to investors, they often find it hard to raise the money needed to grow quickly.

      A The word 'museum' comes from the Greek for a temple of the Muses, the goddesses of the arts, but the modern institution has a more recent origin. These collections were private and were shown only to invited guests.

      B The first public museums appeared in the eighteenth century. The British Museum opened in London in 1759, admitting 'all studious and curious persons' free of charge, although at first visitors had to apply for a ticket in advance. After the French Revolution the royal art collection in the Louvre was opened to the people in 1793. The idea behind these institutions was that knowledge and beauty should not belong only to the rich.

      C For much of their history museums were quiet places where objects sat in glass cases with small labels. Since the late twentieth century many have tried to become more lively, with interactive displays, activities for children and late-night events. Science museums in particular encourage visitors to touch and experiment.

      D What visitors see is only a small part of what a museum owns. Large institutions typically display less than a tenth of their collections; the British Museum, with around eight million objects, shows roughly one per cent at any time. The remainder is kept in storerooms, where it is available to researchers. Many museums are now photographing their holdings and publishing them online, so that an object in a drawer in London or Paris can be examined by a student anywhere in the world.

      E These stored collections sometimes prove valuable in ways their collectors could not have imagined. In the 1960s birds of prey in Britain were mysteriously failing to breed. A scientist, Derek Ratcliffe, measured eggshells that had been gathered by collectors over more than a century and kept in museums. He found that shells laid after 1947 were markedly thinner than earlier ones, the year in which the insecticide DDT had come into general use. The discovery helped to bring about restrictions on the chemical.

      F Whether museums should charge for entry is a matter of long debate. Britain's national museums abolished their entrance fees in 2001, and within a few years the number of visits to those that had previously charged rose by about seventy per cent. Opponents of free entry argue that it is really a subsidy for tourists and for the well-off, who would visit in any case, and surveys do suggest that the social background of visitors changed less than had been hoped.

      G Museums today also face difficult questions about their past. Many famous objects were acquired during the colonial period, sometimes by force. Greece has long asked for the return of the marble sculptures removed from the Parthenon in Athens in the early nineteenth century and now held in London, and Nigeria has requested the Benin Bronzes, taken by British soldiers in 1897. Some museums have begun to send such items back; others argue that they can be seen by more people, and in a wider context, where they are.

Since singing and clapping leave no trace, music itself must be far older.

Darwin proposed that music began as a form of courtship, like birdsong: individuals who sang well attracted mates. Others think it grew out of the soothing sounds that mothers make to infants.       C A third theory emphasises group bonding. When people sing, drum or dance together, they move in time with one another, and experiments show that this synchrony increases trust and willingness to cooperate.       D If music is part of human nature, people everywhere ought to understand one another's songs to some degree, and experiments suggest that they do. Researchers at Harvard assembled recordings from several hundred small societies around the world and played short extracts to listeners in other countries. Without any knowledge of the language or culture, the listeners could usually tell whether a song was a lullaby, a dance or a song for healing. Lullabies everywhere were slow and smooth; dance songs were fast and had a strong beat.

      E The ability to move in time to a beat, which seems so natural to us, is very rare in the animal kingdom. Monkeys cannot be trained to do it reliably.       A On 28 December 1895, in the basement of a Paris café, the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière showed ten short films to a paying audience of about thirty people. Each film lasted less than a minute and showed an everyday scene: workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a gardener being soaked with his own hose. The event is generally regarded as the birth of the cinema.

      B The Lumières were not the only inventors working on moving pictures. In the United States Thomas Edison's company had already produced the Kinetoscope, a box in which one person at a time could watch a film through a small window. The Lumières' machine, the Cinématographe, had two advantages. It projected the image onto a screen, so that many people could watch together, and it was light enough to be carried anywhere, serving as camera, printer and projector in one. A well-known story claims that when the brothers showed a film of a train arriving at a station, spectators ran away in terror; historians now doubt that this ever happened.

      C Curiously, Louis Lumière is said to have believed that the cinema was 'an invention without a future'. It was others who saw its possibilities. Georges Méliès, a professional magician, discovered by accident that stopping the camera could make objects appear to vanish, and he went on to make fantasy films such as A Trip to the Moon in 1902.

      D At first films were shown in fairgrounds, music halls and rented shops. The first building in the United States devoted entirely to them opened in Pittsburgh in 1905. Admission cost five cents, a nickel, and the theatre was named the Nickelodeon. Within three years there were several thousand imitators across the country. Their audiences were largely working people and recent immigrants, for whom the films had a particular attraction: since the stories were told without spoken words, no knowledge of English was needed to follow them.

      E The centre of the American industry was originally New York and its surroundings. Around 1910, film-makers began moving to a quiet suburb of Los Angeles called Hollywood. Southern California offered sunshine almost all year, at a time when most filming depended on natural light, and deserts, mountains and ocean all within a short drive. It was also conveniently distant from Thomas Edison, whose company held patents on film equipment and sent agents to pursue those who used it without paying.

      F Early producers did not reveal the names of their actors, fearing that well-known performers would demand higher wages. That policy collapsed in 1910, when the producer Carl Laemmle hired a popular actress, Florence Lawrence, and spread a false newspaper story that she had been killed in an accident. He then announced indignantly that she was alive and would appear in his next film. Crowds gathered to see her, and the film star was born.

      G For three decades films had no recorded dialogue, though they were rarely silent, since a pianist or orchestra played in the cinema. The Jazz Singer of 1927 was the first feature film with synchronised speech, and within a few years silent films had disappeared.

By the 1970s tags had grown into huge, colourful paintings covering whole train carriages.

      C Another artist who moved from the underground to the gallery was Keith Haring. In the early 1980s he noticed that unused advertising panels in New York subway stations were covered with sheets of black paper, and he began filling them with quick chalk drawings of dancing figures, barking dogs and crawling babies.       D Perhaps the most famous painted surface of all was the Berlin Wall. On its western side, which could be approached freely, people began writing slogans and painting pictures in the late 1970s, until the concrete was covered for kilometres. The eastern side, guarded by soldiers, remained blank. After the wall was opened in 1989, more than a hundred artists from twenty-one countries were invited to paint a surviving section 1.3 kilometres long. Known as the East Side Gallery, it is now a protected monument.

      E Cities have gradually learned to distinguish between kinds of wall painting. Many now provide 'legal walls' where anyone may paint without permission, in the hope of drawing writers away from trains and private property. Evidence on whether this works is mixed. Some studies report less unwanted graffiti nearby, while others find that legal walls simply attract more painters to the district.

      F Since then a broader movement known as street art has developed, using stencils, posters and sculpture as well as spray paint, and usually aiming to communicate with the public rather than with other writers. Its best-known figure is the British artist Banksy, whose identity has never been officially confirmed. His images, often humorous and political, appear overnight, and they are now so valuable that walls bearing them have been cut out and sold.

      G This success has created a paradox. An art form that began as illegal rebellion is now used by city councils to attract tourists and by property developers to make neighbourhoods fashionable. Districts once considered dangerous, such as Shoreditch in London, have become expensive partly because of their murals, and the artists who painted them can often no longer afford to live there.

In 1770 an inventor at the Austrian court unveiled a wooden figure in Turkish dress, seated at a cabinet full of gears, which played a strong game and defeated many opponents during decades of tours through Europe and America. Napoleon is said to have been among them. The 'Turk' was in fact a trick: a skilled human player was concealed inside the cabinet.

      F Chess has long been used as a test of machine intelligence. In 1997 the IBM computer Deep Blue defeated the world champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match, an event reported around the world. Deep Blue relied on calculating some 200 million positions per second. Twenty years later a program called AlphaZero took a different approach: given only the rules, it taught itself by playing millions of games against itself, and within hours it could beat the strongest existing programs.

      G Far from killing the game, computers have helped it to flourish. Players use programs to train, and online platforms allow anyone to find an opponent at any hour.       A There are roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, but they are very unequally distributed. About half of the world's population speaks one of just twenty-five languages, while several thousand languages have fewer than ten thousand speakers each. Linguists estimate that at least forty per cent of all languages are endangered, and that one disappears, on average, every few weeks when its last speaker dies.

      B Linguistic variety is greatest in regions where mountains, forests or islands have kept communities apart. The extreme case is Papua New Guinea, where about 840 languages are spoken by a population of some nine million, more than in the whole of Europe and the Americas combined. Many are used by only a few hundred people in a single valley, and neighbouring villages may be unable to understand each other.

      C Counting languages is less straightforward than it sounds, because there is no agreed way of distinguishing a language from a dialect. Danish, Norwegian and Swedish are regarded as separate languages although their speakers can usually follow one another, whereas the forms of Chinese spoken in Beijing and Hong Kong are officially dialects, yet differ as much as Spanish does from Italian. As one scholar remarked, a language is a dialect with an army and a navy: the decision is often political.

      D The end, when it comes, can be dated precisely. Eyak, once spoken on the southern coast of Alaska, died on 21 January 2008 with its last native speaker, Marie Smith Jones, at the age of eighty-nine. For years she had had nobody to converse with in her mother tongue except a visiting linguist, with whom she worked to compile a dictionary. None of her nine children had learned the language, because, as she explained, when they were young it was considered wrong to speak anything but English.

      E Languages rarely die because their speakers do. More commonly, a community shifts to a more powerful language that offers better access to education and work. Parents stop using the old language with their children, believing they are helping them to succeed, and within two or three generations it is gone. In the past the process was often forced. In Australia, Canada and the United States, indigenous children were sent to boarding schools where they were punished for speaking their mother tongue.

      F Why should this loss concern anyone else? Each language is a unique record of how a group of people has understood the world. Many contain detailed knowledge of local plants, animals and weather that exists nowhere else. For the speakers themselves, language is closely tied to identity and to the stories and songs of their ancestors.

      G Decline is not always final. Hebrew, which for almost two thousand years had been used mainly for prayer and study, was revived as an everyday spoken language at the end of the nineteenth century and now has millions of native speakers. Welsh and Maori have been strengthened by schools that teach entirely in those languages. Technology is helping too: linguists record elderly speakers, and communities are creating dictionaries and learning apps.

      A The earliest bridges were probably tree trunks laid across streams, and in principle the simple beam bridge has not changed: a horizontal structure resting on supports at each end. Its weakness is length. A long beam sags in the middle, so beam bridges need many supports.

      B The Romans overcame this with the arch. In a stone arch each block presses against its neighbours, so the load is carried outwards and down into the ground. Roman arches were so well built that some, like the Pont du Gard in southern France, are still standing after two thousand years. Arches, however, require a great quantity of stone and solid foundations on both sides.

      C New materials changed what was possible. In 1779 the world's first large bridge of cast iron was completed across the River Severn at Coalbrookdale in England, the centre of the early iron industry. Its builders had no experience of the material and joined the parts in the way carpenters join timber, yet the bridge still stands. Iron allowed longer, lighter spans than stone, but cast iron is brittle, and a series of failures followed.

      D The worst occurred in Scotland on a stormy night in December 1879, when the central section of the railway bridge over the River Tay collapsed as a train was crossing; all seventy-five people on board were lost. The designers of the next great Scottish bridge, across the Forth, were determined that it should not only be safe but look safe. Opened in 1890 and built of steel on the cantilever principle, with huge arms balanced on three towers, it used ten times as much metal as a modern engineer would consider necessary. It remains in daily use.

      E Not every bridge is built; a few are grown. In the wet hills of north-eastern India, where wooden structures quickly rot, the Khasi people guide the roots of a kind of fig tree across streams along hollow trunks or bamboo poles. After fifteen years or more the roots are thick enough to bear the weight of a person, and they go on strengthening for as long as the tree lives. Some of these living bridges are believed to be several centuries old.

      F The widest gaps are crossed by suspension bridges, in which the roadway hangs from cables stretched between tall towers. The idea is ancient: the Incas of South America built suspension bridges of woven grass across mountain gorges. Modern versions use steel. When the Brooklyn Bridge opened in New York in 1883, it was by far the longest in the world, and many people feared it would fall. To reassure them, a circus owner is said to have led twenty-one elephants across it the following year.

      G Suspension bridges are light and flexible, and this can be a danger. In 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in the United States began to twist violently in a moderate wind and collapsed just four months after opening; the only victim was a dog. Since then, designs have been tested in wind tunnels. The current record holder, the 1915 Çanakkale Bridge in Turkey, opened in 2022, has a main span of just over two kilometres.

      A The oldest surviving photograph was taken in 1826 or 1827 by a French inventor, Nicéphore Niépce, from an upstairs window of his country house. It shows, rather faintly, the roofs of the surrounding buildings. The exposure took at least eight hours, so that sunlight appears on both sides of the courtyard.

      B Niépce's partner Louis Daguerre developed a far more practical process, which the French government bought and presented 'free to the world' in 1839. A daguerreotype produced a wonderfully sharp image on a silvered metal plate. Exposure times soon fell to under a minute, and portrait studios opened in cities everywhere. For the first time ordinary families could own an accurate likeness of a relative. The method had limits, though: each picture was unique and could not be copied, and sitters had to keep perfectly still, which is one reason why people in early photographs rarely smile.

      C In England, meanwhile, William Henry Fox Talbot had invented a process that produced a negative on paper, from which any number of positive prints could be made. This principle became the basis of photography for the next 150 years.

      D The camera was soon taken to war. In 1855 the Englishman Roger Fenton travelled to the Crimea with a wagon converted into a darkroom, since each glass plate had to be prepared and developed on the spot. Exposures of several seconds made it impossible to record fighting, and his pictures show camps, officers and empty battlefields. Seven years later, during the American Civil War, an exhibition in New York of photographs of the dead lying where they had fallen shocked a public accustomed to heroic paintings.

      E Photography also revealed things too quick for the eye. For centuries artists had painted galloping horses with their legs stretched out in front and behind. In 1878, to settle a question raised by a wealthy horse owner, the photographer Eadweard Muybridge set up twelve cameras in a row beside a racetrack in California, each triggered by a thread that the horse broke as it passed. The pictures proved that all four hooves do leave the ground at once, but when they are gathered under the body, not stretched out.

      F Colour proved a harder problem. The first commercially successful process was introduced in 1907 by the Lumiere brothers, better known as pioneers of the cinema. Their glass plates were coated with millions of microscopic grains of potato starch dyed red, green and blue, which acted as tiny filters. The results were soft and beautiful but needed long exposures, and colour did not become common in family albums until the 1960s.

      G Photography remained a business for professionals until 1888, when the American George Eastman launched the Kodak camera with the slogan 'You press the button, we do the rest'. It came loaded with a roll of film for a hundred pictures; the customer posted the whole camera back to the factory for developing. Photography became a popular hobby. The latest revolution began in 1975, when an engineer at Eastman's own company built the first digital camera. Ironically, the firm was slow to develop the idea, and in 2012 it was declared bankrupt.

      A Games in which a ball is kicked have been played for thousands of years. In China a game called cuju, in which players kicked a leather ball through an opening in a net, was popular more than two thousand years ago. In medieval England, 'mob football' was played between whole villages, with hundreds of players, few rules and frequent injuries. Several kings tried to ban it, without success.

      B The modern game was shaped in English private schools in the early nineteenth century. Each school had its own version: at some the ball could be carried, at others only kicked. This caused confusion whenever former pupils from different schools wanted to play together. On 26 October 1863 representatives of a number of clubs met at a London tavern and founded the Football Association to agree on a single set of rules. The crucial decision was to forbid carrying the ball and kicking opponents' legs. Clubs that disagreed left and later developed the separate game of rugby.

      C Football spread quickly among industrial workers, who by then had Saturday afternoons free, and many famous clubs began as teams from factories or churches. British sailors, engineers and traders carried the game abroad, especially to South America and continental Europe. The international governing body, FIFA, was founded in Paris in 1904, and the first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, when the host nation won.

      D The rules agreed in 1863 have been modified many times. Early matches had no referee on the pitch: the two captains settled disputes between themselves, on the assumption that gentlemen would not cheat. As competition grew fiercer, that assumption could not last. The penalty kick was introduced in 1891 at the suggestion of an Irish goalkeeper, William McCrum, and was at first bitterly opposed by amateur clubs, who considered it an insult to suggest that a player might foul deliberately.

      E Yellow and red cards arrived much later. During the 1966 World Cup a player who had been sent off refused to leave the field, partly because he and the referee had no language in common. Ken Aston, the English official in charge of referees, was driving home afterwards when he stopped at a set of traffic lights and saw the solution: yellow for caution, red for stop. The cards were first used at the World Cup of 1970.

      F The women's game has had a more troubled history. During the First World War, teams formed by women working in English factories played matches for charity, and one of them drew a crowd of 53,000 in Liverpool in 1920. The following year the Football Association declared the sport unsuitable for women and banned them from its members' grounds. The ban was not lifted until 1971. The first official Women's World Cup was held twenty years after that, in China.

      G The game's success owes much to its simplicity. It needs only a ball and some open ground, and its basic rules can be explained in a minute. Today it is estimated that several billion people follow the World Cup, making it the most watched sporting event on Earth.

      A Elephants are the largest animals living on land, and among the most intelligent. An African elephant's brain weighs about five kilograms, more than that of any other land animal. But what impresses researchers most is not the size of the brain; it is the complexity of elephant society.

      B The basic unit is the family, a group of related females and their young led by the oldest female, known as the matriarch. Males leave the family in their early teens and live alone or in loose groups with other males. The matriarch's experience is vital. She remembers the location of water holes that may be needed only once in many years, and studies in Kenya have shown that families led by older matriarchs are better at recognising the roar of a dangerous lion. During a severe drought in Tanzania in 1993, groups with older leaders lost far fewer calves, apparently because the leaders remembered a previous drought and led their families to distant food.

      C Elephants communicate constantly. Besides trumpeting, they produce deep rumbles, many of them too low for humans to hear, which can travel several kilometres. They show what looks very much like emotion. They greet returning relatives with obvious excitement, help injured companions, and show a striking interest in the bones of dead elephants, touching them gently with their trunks.

      D The elephant's most distinctive feature, its trunk, is a combined nose and upper lip containing tens of thousands of individual muscles and no bones. It is strong enough to push over a tree and delicate enough to pick up a single peanut. An elephant uses it to breathe, drink, feed, wash, greet and threaten, and as a snorkel when swimming. The sense of smell it provides is among the keenest known: elephants can detect water several kilometres away and can distinguish between human groups that have hunted them and groups that have not, simply from the scent of their clothing.

      E In 2006 researchers at a zoo in New York tested whether elephants recognise themselves in a mirror, an ability previously demonstrated only in great apes, dolphins and humans. A white cross was painted on the forehead of an Asian elephant called Happy, in a place she could not see directly. Standing in front of a large mirror, she repeatedly touched the mark with the tip of her trunk. She had understood that the animal in the glass was herself.

      F Elephants also shape the landscape for other species. In dry seasons they dig into river beds with their feet and tusks to reach water, creating pools that many animals depend on. By pushing over trees they keep grassland open, and they swallow fruit whole and deposit the seeds, complete with fertiliser, many kilometres away. Some trees of the African rainforest have seeds so large that no other animal can spread them.

      G Their future is uncertain. In the early twentieth century Africa may have held several million elephants; today there are about 415,000. Poaching for ivory killed vast numbers, and although the international ivory trade was banned in 1989, illegal hunting continues. An increasing problem is conflict with farmers, as expanding villages and fields leave elephants less room.

      A The emperor penguin is the largest of all penguins, standing more than a metre tall, and it breeds in the harshest conditions faced by any bird. While other Antarctic animals raise their young in the brief summer, emperors do so in the depths of winter, on the sea ice, in darkness, with temperatures falling below minus forty degrees and winds of over 150 kilometres an hour.

      B The cycle begins in autumn, when the birds walk as much as a hundred kilometres inland to their colonies. The female lays a single egg and immediately passes it to the male, who balances it on his feet beneath a warm fold of skin. She then returns to the sea to feed. For about two months the male keeps the egg warm. He eats nothing during this time and may lose almost half his body weight.

      C To survive, the males cooperate. Thousands crowd together in a tight huddle, which may be twenty degrees or more warmer in the centre than outside. The huddle is constantly in motion: birds on the cold outer edge gradually work their way inwards while those in the middle move out, so that each takes a turn in the warmth.

      D The females come back around the time the chicks hatch and take over, and the hungry males finally leave to feed. The timing of the whole cycle means that the young are ready to swim in summer, when the ice edge is close and food is abundant.

      E Once the chicks are a few weeks old, both parents must fish to satisfy them, and the young are left together in large groups for warmth and protection. A returning adult therefore faces the problem of finding one chick among thousands that look identical. The solution is sound. Every emperor penguin has a call with its own pattern, produced by two voices at once, and a chick can pick out its parent's call from the din of the colony within seconds.

      F At sea the clumsy walker becomes a superb swimmer. Emperor penguins hunt fish, squid and small shrimp-like animals beneath the ice, and they dive deeper than any other bird. Instruments attached to their backs have recorded descents of more than five hundred metres and dives lasting over twenty minutes. Unlike flying birds, whose bones are hollow, penguins have solid bones, which help them to sink.

      G Because the colonies lie in some of the least accessible places on Earth, nobody knew how many emperors existed until scientists turned to satellites. The birds themselves are too small to see from space, but their droppings stain the ice a reddish brown, and these patches show up clearly in photographs. A survey completed in 2012 located forty-six colonies, several of them previously unknown, and put the total at about 600,000 birds, roughly twice the earlier estimate.

      H Because emperors depend on stable sea ice for most of the year, they are highly exposed to a warming climate. In 2022 several colonies in one region lost almost all their chicks when the ice broke up before the young had grown waterproof feathers.

      A The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, covering about nine million square kilometres, an area nearly as large as the United States. The popular image is of endless sand dunes, but sand seas make up only around a fifth of it. Most of the Sahara consists of bare rock, gravel plains and mountains, some rising above 3,000 metres.

      B Daytime temperatures in summer regularly exceed forty-five degrees, yet nights can be cold, because dry air and clear skies let heat escape quickly. Rain is rare and unpredictable; some areas receive none for years. Life has nevertheless adapted. The fennec fox loses heat through its enormous ears, and the camel can go for a week or more without drinking.

      C People have lived in this unpromising environment for thousands of years. The Tuareg, nomadic herders sometimes called the 'blue people' because the dye of their robes stains the skin, traditionally moved with their camels and goats between seasonal pastures and controlled the caravan routes. Settled life is possible only at oases, where underground water reaches the surface or can be led to it through hand-dug tunnels. There, in the shade of date palms, farmers grow fruit, vegetables and grain in gardens no larger than a tennis court.

      D On the southern edge of the desert stands Timbuktu, a name that in English has come to mean the most remote place imaginable. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries it was one of the great centres of learning of the Islamic world, with a university that attracted thousands of students. Hundreds of thousands of handwritten books on law, astronomy and medicine have been preserved by local families ever since. When armed groups occupied the city in 2012, librarians smuggled most of the manuscripts to safety in metal trunks, hidden under sacks of vegetables.

      E The desert holds curiosities of another kind. In the far south-west of Egypt the sand is scattered with pieces of a pale yellow natural glass, formed some 29 million years ago when a meteorite, or its explosion in the air, melted the surface. The ancient Egyptians valued it: a beetle carved from this glass forms the centrepiece of a jewel found in the tomb of Tutankhamun.

      F Remarkably, the Sahara was not always a desert. Rock paintings in the mountains of Algeria and Libya, thousands of years old, show giraffes, elephants, hippos and people swimming. Between about 11,000 and 5,000 years ago the region was a grassland with lakes and rivers. This 'Green Sahara' was the result of a slight change in the tilt of the Earth's axis, which moved the African monsoon rains northwards. When the rains shifted south again, the land dried out within a few centuries, and many of its people moved towards the Nile valley, which may have contributed to the rise of Egyptian civilisation.

      G The Sahara affects places far beyond Africa. Each year winds lift hundreds of millions of tonnes of dust from it. Some of this crosses the Atlantic and falls on the Amazon rainforest, where the phosphorus it contains helps to fertilise the soil. On the desert's southern edge, African nations are planting a belt of trees and vegetation, the Great Green Wall, to stop farmland from turning to desert.

      A By the amount of water it carries, the Amazon is easily the greatest river on Earth. It discharges about a fifth of all the fresh water that rivers pour into the oceans, more than the next seven largest rivers combined. So powerful is the flow that fresh water can be found on the surface of the Atlantic more than a hundred kilometres from the shore. Whether the Amazon or the Nile is the longer river is still disputed, since it depends on which stream is counted as the source; both are well over 6,000 kilometres.

      B The river rises high in the Andes of Peru, less than 200 kilometres from the Pacific Ocean, and flows east across the whole width of South America. More than a thousand tributaries join it. There is not a single bridge across the main river along its entire length, mainly because it passes through thinly populated forest where there are few roads to connect.

      C Each year, rains in the Andes cause the river to rise by as much as fifteen metres, flooding an area of forest larger than England for months at a time. Fish swim among the tree trunks and feed on fallen fruit, spreading the seeds. The river is home to more species of fish than any other, probably over 3,000, along with pink river dolphins, giant otters and the piranha, whose danger to humans is greatly exaggerated.

      D The river owes its name to a sixteenth-century Spanish soldier, Francisco de Orellana, who in 1541 and 1542 became the first European to travel its whole length. He reported being attacked by a tribe led by women warriors, and the river was named after the Amazons, the female fighters of Greek legend. Orellana also described large towns and well-kept roads along the banks. Later travellers found only forest, and his account was dismissed as fantasy. In recent years, however, aircraft carrying laser scanners that can see through the trees have revealed the remains of extensive settlements, causeways and reservoirs, suggesting that he may have been telling the truth.

      E Twice a day the Atlantic takes a small revenge on the river. Around the time of the highest tides, the incoming sea overcomes the current at the mouth and a wave up to four metres high rushes upstream with a roar that can be heard half an hour before it arrives. Local people call it the pororoca, and surfers travel from around the world to ride it; the longest rides have lasted more than thirty minutes.

      F The forest and the river are more closely linked than might appear. An individual large tree can draw several hundred litres of water from the soil in a day and release it through its leaves. Added together, the trees of the basin send about twenty billion tonnes of water vapour into the air daily, more than the river itself carries to the sea. Winds carry these 'flying rivers' south, where they fall as rain on the farms and cities of southern Brazil.

      G The Amazon has been a highway for people for thousands of years, and ocean-going ships can travel upstream as far as the Peruvian city of Iquitos, some 3,600 kilometres from the sea. Today dams on its tributaries, gold mining that pollutes the water with mercury, and the clearing of the surrounding forest all threaten the system.

      A Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent. The lowest natural temperature ever measured at ground level, minus 89.2 degrees Celsius, was recorded at the Russian Vostok station in 1983. Although about ninety-eight per cent of the land is covered by ice, so little snow falls in the interior that it technically counts as a desert. The ice sheet is on average about two kilometres thick, and it holds roughly seventy per cent of the planet's fresh water.

      B No human set eyes on the continent until 1820, and the first people reached the South Pole in December 1911, when a Norwegian team led by Roald Amundsen arrived five weeks ahead of the British expedition under Robert Scott. Scott and his four companions died on the return journey.

      C Antarctica has no permanent inhabitants and belongs to no country. Under the Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 and now accepted by more than fifty states, the continent is reserved for peaceful purposes. Military activity is prohibited, and a later agreement forbids mining. Several thousand scientists and support staff live at research stations in summer, falling to about a thousand in the dark winter months.

      D The continent itself supports almost no life. There are no trees or shrubs, only mosses and lichens on the few patches of bare rock, and the largest animal that spends its whole life on land is a wingless insect about six millimetres long. The surrounding ocean, by contrast, is extraordinarily rich. Its cold waters hold immense swarms of krill, small shrimp-like creatures that are the main food of the whales, seals, penguins and seabirds for which the region is famous.

      E Beneath the ice lies a hidden world. Radar surveys have identified more than four hundred lakes under the ice sheet, kept liquid by heat from the Earth's interior and by the pressure of the ice above. The largest, Lake Vostok, is about the size of Lake Ontario and lies under almost four kilometres of ice; it has been sealed off from the atmosphere for millions of years. In 2012, after two decades of drilling, a Russian team finally reached its surface. Scientists hope that any organisms living in such lakes may show what kind of life could exist on the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn.

      F Scientists are no longer the only visitors. About 100,000 tourists now travel to Antarctica each summer, most of them by ship from the southern tip of South America. Operators follow strict rules: boots are disinfected before every landing to avoid introducing foreign seeds, no more than a hundred passengers may go ashore at one place at a time, and visitors must keep at least five metres from wildlife.

      G Their research is of global importance. Ice drilled from deep within the sheet contains tiny bubbles of ancient air, providing a record of the atmosphere going back 800,000 years. It was in Antarctica, in 1985, that British scientists discovered the hole in the ozone layer, a finding that led to an international ban on the chemicals responsible. Today attention is fixed on the stability of the ice itself: if the West Antarctic ice sheet were to melt entirely, global sea level would rise by several metres.

      A For a long time the use of tools was thought to be a uniquely human ability, and later one shared only with apes. Then scientists turned their attention to the crow family. On the Pacific island of New Caledonia lives a crow that not only uses tools but manufactures them. It strips twigs and shapes them into hooks, and tears strips from the edges of tough leaves, in order to pull insects out of holes in wood. Different populations on the island produce tools of different designs, which suggests that the techniques are learned from other birds.

      B The most famous individual was a captive New Caledonian crow named Betty, studied at Oxford University. In 2002 she was given a straight piece of wire and a small bucket of food at the bottom of a tube. Without any training, Betty bent the wire into a hook and lifted the bucket out.

      C Other experiments recall a fable by the ancient Greek writer Aesop, in which a thirsty crow drops pebbles into a jug to raise the water. Real crows presented with a tube of water and a floating piece of food do exactly this, and they choose heavy objects that sink rather than light ones that float. Crows in a Japanese city have been filmed placing nuts on the road for cars to crack and waiting for the traffic lights to change before collecting them.

      D Members of the crow family may even think ahead. In an experiment in Sweden, ravens were taught to use a particular stone to open a box containing food. Later the box was removed, and the birds were offered a choice of objects, among them the stone. Most took it and kept it, and when the box was brought back, as much as seventeen hours afterwards, they used it at once. In a further test the ravens turned down a small immediate treat in favour of a token that they could later exchange for a better one, a kind of self-control that human children do not show reliably until they are about four.

      E Crows gather noisily around the body of a dead companion, behaviour sometimes described as a funeral. Experiments indicate that the purpose is practical. When researchers placed a stuffed crow on the ground with a masked person standing nearby, the birds mobbed the person on later occasions and for several days avoided food put out at that spot. They appear to treat a death as a warning and to gather in order to learn what caused it.

      F Their relations with people are not always hostile. An eight-year-old American girl who had fed the crows in her garden every day began to find small objects left on the feeding tray: buttons, beads, a paper clip, a single earring, a tiny silver heart. Biologists cannot be sure that such offerings are intended as gifts, but there are many similar reports.

      G Crows also have excellent memories for people. Researchers in Seattle who wore a particular mask while trapping crows found that the birds scolded anyone wearing that mask for years afterwards. Even crows that had not been born at the time joined in, having apparently learned from their elders whom to distrust.
