      A In 1967 the biologist Roger Payne and his colleague Scott McVay made a remarkable discovery while analysing underwater recordings made near Bermuda. The long, eerie sounds produced by humpback whales were not random. They were arranged in repeated patterns, in the same way as the song of a bird, although on a far larger scale. A single song may last up to half an hour, and a whale may repeat it for many hours.

      B Only the males sing, mostly in the warm waters where humpbacks gather to breed, so the songs are thought to be connected with mating, though exactly how is unclear. They may attract females, or they may be a means by which males compete with or keep track of one another.

      C The most extraordinary feature is the way the songs change. All the males in one population sing the same song, but it gradually evolves through the season as new phrases are added and old ones dropped. Occasionally something more dramatic happens. Researchers studying whales off eastern Australia found that within two years the entire population had abandoned its song and adopted a completely different one, which had been introduced by a small number of visitors from the Indian Ocean. Such songs then spread eastwards across the South Pacific from one population to the next. Scientists have described this as one of the clearest examples of culture in animals.

      D Song is not the only behaviour that humpbacks pass on. In the cold waters where they feed, groups of whales cooperate in an ingenious method of catching fish. One or more animals swim in a circle beneath a shoal, blowing a continuous stream of bubbles that rises like a curtain and frightens the fish into a tight ball. The whales then surge up through the centre with their mouths open. Off the north-east coast of the United States, a new variation, in which the whale first slaps the surface with its tail, was seen in a single animal in 1980 and within thirty years had spread to hundreds.

      E The voices of the largest whales carry astonishing distances. Blue and fin whales produce notes so deep that most are below the range of human hearing, and in a particular layer of the ocean, where temperature and pressure trap sound, such calls can travel for more than a thousand kilometres. Before the age of engines, a whale may have been able to hear others across an entire ocean basin.

      F One voice has puzzled listeners for decades. In 1989 underwater microphones belonging to the American navy picked up a whale calling at a pitch far higher than that of any known species. The same call has been followed across the North Pacific year after year, always alone. Nobody has ever seen the animal that makes it. Newspapers named it the loneliest whale in the world, although scientists point out that other whales can probably hear it perfectly well.

      G Payne's recordings were released as an album in 1970 and became an unexpected bestseller. The public response helped to bring about the international ban on commercial whaling in 1986, and humpback numbers have since recovered strongly. The whales now face a different threat: the noise of ships, which can drown out their songs.

      A Few animals are as well adapted to their environment as the camel. There are two domesticated species: the one-humped dromedary of Arabia and North Africa, and the two-humped Bactrian camel of Central Asia, which can endure winters of minus thirty degrees as well as summer heat.

      B Contrary to popular belief, a camel's hump does not hold water. It is a store of fat, weighing up to thirty-six kilograms, which the animal draws on when food is scarce. Keeping its fat in one place instead of spreading it under the skin helps the camel to stay cool.

      C Its ability to cope without water depends on several other features. A camel can lose up to a quarter of its body weight in water without harm, a loss that would kill most mammals. Its body temperature can vary by about six degrees during the day, so it does not begin to sweat until the air is very hot. Its kidneys produce highly concentrated urine, and its nostrils recover moisture from the air it breathes out. When water is finally available, a thirsty camel can drink more than a hundred litres in around ten minutes. Long eyelashes and nostrils that can close protect it from blowing sand, and broad, padded feet stop it from sinking into soft ground.

      D Surprisingly, the camel family began not in Asia or Africa but in North America, about forty-five million years ago. Fossil bones of a giant camel have even been found in the Canadian Arctic, which was then covered by forest. Some members of the family later wandered south and became the llamas of the Andes; others walked into Asia across a bridge of land that once joined Alaska to Siberia. In their original homeland camels died out around ten thousand years ago.

      E Today the largest population of wild camels lives on a continent where they are not native at all. From the 1840s onwards, thousands were shipped to Australia, together with experienced handlers from South Asia, to carry supplies for explorers and for the builders of railways and telegraph lines across the dry interior. When lorries replaced them in the 1920s, many were simply turned loose. Their descendants now number several hundred thousand, and they damage water holes and vegetation to such an extent that the government organises regular culls.

      F The truly wild camel, by contrast, is one of the rarest large mammals on Earth. Fewer than a thousand wild Bactrian camels survive in the Gobi Desert of China and Mongolia. Genetic studies have shown that they are not escaped domestic animals but a separate species, and they possess one extraordinary ability: they can drink water that is saltier than the sea.

      G Camels were domesticated more than three thousand years ago, and they transformed life in dry regions. A loaded camel can walk around forty kilometres a day, and without camels the caravan trade across the Sahara and along the Silk Road would have been impossible. Today they are still valued for milk, meat and wool, and scientists are studying the unusually small antibodies in camel blood for use in medicine.

      A Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the boundary where the North American and Eurasian plates are slowly moving apart. As a result the island has about thirty active volcanic systems and hundreds of hot springs. The English word 'geyser' comes from Geysir, the name of a famous spouting spring in the south of the country.

      B Extracting the heat is simple in principle. Engineers drill wells two or three kilometres deep into rock that is still hot from volcanic activity. Water under pressure rushes to the surface, where part of it flashes into steam and drives turbines; the remaining hot water is piped to towns. The cooled water is afterwards pumped back underground so that the supply is not exhausted. Pipelines carrying water to the capital are so well insulated that the temperature falls by only about two degrees over a distance of twenty-seven kilometres.

      C Living on a volcanic island has obvious risks. In January 1973 a fissure opened without warning on the edge of the only town on the island of Heimaey, off the south coast, and the entire population of 5,000 was taken to the mainland overnight by the fishing fleet, which happened to be in port because of a storm. Over the following months lava buried a third of the town and threatened to close the harbour on which its living depended. In a bold experiment, workers pumped millions of tonnes of seawater onto the advancing lava to cool and harden it. The harbour was saved, and most of the islanders returned.

      D Icelandic engineers are now using their rocks in a new way. At a power station near Reykjavik, carbon dioxide is dissolved in water and injected deep into the volcanic basalt, where it reacts with minerals and turns to solid stone in less than two years. The method offers a permanent means of storing a gas that would otherwise warm the atmosphere.

      E For centuries Icelanders used the hot water mainly for washing and bathing. Houses were heated with peat and, later, with imported coal, and photographs of the capital, Reykjavik, from the early twentieth century show a city under a cloud of smoke. The change began in the 1930s, when hot water was first piped to a school and some nearby houses. The oil crisis of the 1970s, which sharply raised the cost of imported fuel, persuaded the government to extend the system across the country.

      F Today about nine out of ten Icelandic homes are heated directly with geothermal water. Almost all of the nation's electricity is renewable as well, roughly seventy per cent coming from hydroelectric dams and thirty per cent from geothermal power stations. The warm water has other uses. Pavements and car parks in Reykjavik are heated from below to keep them free of ice, greenhouses grow tomatoes and even bananas close to the Arctic Circle, and outdoor swimming pools are open all year.

      G Cheap, clean electricity has attracted energy-hungry industries, particularly aluminium smelting and data centres. Not all Icelanders welcome this, since new power stations and dams change wild landscapes that are valued for their own sake and for tourism. Iceland's experience cannot simply be copied elsewhere, but its engineers now advise geothermal projects in East Africa, Asia and beyond.

      A In 1960 the Aral Sea, lying between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was the fourth largest lake in the world, with an area of about 68,000 square kilometres. Fishing fleets working from ports such as Moynaq and Aralsk landed tens of thousands of tonnes of fish a year. Sixty years later most of it had become desert.

      B The sea was fed by two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya. In the 1960s Soviet planners decided to use their water to irrigate vast new fields of cotton and rice in the surrounding dry lands. Thousands of kilometres of canals were dug, many of them unlined, so that a large part of the water soaked into the sand or evaporated before it reached the crops. With far less water arriving, the sea began to shrink. By the late 1980s it had split in two, and by the 2010s it had lost about ninety per cent of its volume.

      C The results were disastrous. As the water grew saltier, the native fish died and the fishing industry collapsed; rusting ships now lie on dry sand far from any shore. The exposed seabed, covered in salt and residues of farm chemicals, is swept by winds that carry toxic dust over a wide region, and rates of breathing and other illnesses among local people have risen. Without the moderating influence of the water, summers have become hotter and winters colder.

      D For the people of the region the change was swift and bewildering. The town of Moynaq, on the southern shore, had been a busy port with a fish cannery that employed several thousand workers. As the water withdrew, a channel was dug to keep the harbour connected to the sea, then extended, and finally abandoned. For some years the cannery was kept working with frozen fish brought by rail from the Baltic and the Pacific, thousands of kilometres away, before it closed. The shoreline is now more than a hundred kilometres from the town.

      E The retreat of the water exposed another legacy of the period. An island in the middle of the sea had been used since the 1940s as a secret testing ground for biological weapons, chosen precisely because it was so isolated. As the sea shrank, the island grew, and by 2001 it had joined the mainland, so that animals, and people, could walk onto it. The following year an international team spent several months destroying the stores of anthrax that had been buried there.

      F The underlying cause, the demand for irrigation water, is slowly being addressed. Uzbekistan, long one of the world's largest exporters of cotton, has reduced the area planted with the crop in favour of fruit, vegetables and wheat, which need less water and earn more. Farmers are being helped to line canals with concrete and to install drip systems, and the state no longer sets a compulsory quota for the cotton harvest.

      G There has been a partial recovery in the north. A dam completed by Kazakhstan in 2005, with support from the World Bank, raised the level of the small northern sea, and fish and fishermen have returned. The larger southern part is unlikely to be restored. In Uzbekistan, efforts now focus on planting hardy saxaul shrubs on the dry seabed to hold down the dust.

      A Mars has fascinated humanity for centuries. In the 1890s the American astronomer Percival Lowell announced that he could see canals on its surface, built, he believed, by an intelligent civilisation struggling to survive on a drying planet. The canals turned out to be an optical illusion, but the idea of Martians has never quite left the popular imagination.

      B The real Mars is a harsh place. It is about half the diameter of the Earth, and its thin atmosphere, composed almost entirely of carbon dioxide, has less than one per cent of the pressure of ours. The average temperature is around minus sixty degrees. Yet it was not always so. Photographs from orbit show dry river valleys and deltas, and robot vehicles on the surface have found minerals that form only in water. Billions of years ago Mars had lakes and perhaps an ocean. Whether life ever arose there is the central question that current missions are trying to answer.

      C Mars is also a world of spectacular scenery. Its largest volcano, Olympus Mons, rises about twenty-two kilometres above the surrounding plain, two and a half times the height of Everest, and covers an area the size of Italy. A system of canyons near the equator stretches for 4,000 kilometres, roughly the distance from one coast of the United States to the other. A day on Mars lasts only about forty minutes longer than a day on Earth, but gravity is little more than a third as strong, and dust storms occasionally grow until they hide the entire planet for weeks.

      D Our knowledge comes largely from a series of robot vehicles. The first, which landed in 1997, was no bigger than a microwave oven and travelled about a hundred metres. Its successors have grown steadily larger and more capable. Perseverance, which arrived in 2021, is the size of a small car and carries a drill, with which it is filling metal tubes with samples of rock for a future mission to bring back to Earth. It has also performed an experiment of great importance for human visitors, producing small quantities of oxygen from the carbon dioxide of the Martian air.

      E Perseverance brought a passenger: a helicopter weighing less than two kilograms. Because the air is so thin, its blades had to spin many times faster than those of a helicopter on Earth. In April 2021 it made the first powered flight on another planet, rising three metres and hovering for half a minute. It had been designed to fly five times. By the time a damaged blade ended its career in early 2024, it had made seventy-two flights.

      F Sending people is far more difficult than sending machines. Because of the way the planets move, a journey is practical only about once every twenty-six months, and it takes six to nine months each way. Astronauts would be exposed to dangerous radiation, and their muscles and bones would weaken in weightlessness. A radio signal takes up to twenty minutes to reach Earth, so the crew could not rely on immediate help. Landing is particularly hard: the atmosphere is too thin for parachutes alone to slow a heavy spacecraft, yet thick enough to cause intense heating.

      G Space agencies and private companies have nevertheless announced plans to send crews in the coming decades. Critics ask whether the enormous expense is justified when robots are becoming ever more capable.

      A Until the early seventeenth century, everything humans knew about the sky had been learned with the naked eye. In 1609 the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei heard of a Dutch invention that used two lenses to make distant objects appear closer. He built his own improved version and pointed it at the night sky. Within months he had seen mountains on the Moon, four moons circling Jupiter and countless stars invisible to the eye. His observations supported the idea, dangerous at the time, that the Earth is not the centre of the universe.

      B Telescopes with lenses suffered from a defect: they surrounded bright objects with fringes of false colour. In 1668 Isaac Newton solved the problem by using a curved mirror instead of a lens to gather the light. Nearly all large telescopes since then have been reflectors, because mirrors can be made much bigger than lenses. The bigger the mirror, the more light it collects and the fainter the objects it can detect.

      C The power of the reflecting telescope was demonstrated by a musician. William Herschel, a German-born organist living in the English city of Bath, taught himself to grind mirrors and built instruments better than those of any professional observatory. In March 1781, while surveying the sky from his back garden, he noticed an object that moved slowly among the stars. It was Uranus, the first planet to be discovered since ancient times. His sister Caroline, who assisted him, became a noted astronomer herself and found eight comets.

      D Light is not the only messenger from space. In 1932 Karl Jansky, an engineer investigating interference on transatlantic telephone lines for an American company, traced a faint steady hiss to the centre of the Milky Way. His discovery was largely ignored at the time, but after the Second World War, astronomers using equipment developed for radar began to map the sky at radio wavelengths. Radio telescopes, which are huge metal dishes, revealed objects that no optical telescope could have detected, among them the rapidly spinning dead stars known as pulsars.

      E Optical telescopes meanwhile continued to grow. A single mirror much more than eight metres across would bend under its own weight, so the largest modern instruments use a mosaic of smaller pieces. Each of the twin Keck telescopes in Hawaii has a mirror ten metres wide made of thirty-six six-sided segments, kept in line by computer. Such giants are built on high, dry mountains, far from city lights.

      F Even the best telescope on the ground must look through the Earth's atmosphere, which blurs the image and blocks some kinds of light entirely. The answer was to go above it. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, at first returned blurred pictures because its main mirror had been ground to very slightly the wrong shape. Astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993, and Hubble went on to transform astronomy.

      G Its successor, the James Webb Space Telescope, was launched in December 2021. With a gold-coated mirror 6.5 metres across, it observes infrared light and orbits the Sun 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. It can see galaxies as they were more than thirteen billion years ago, soon after the universe began.

      A Chocolate is made from the seeds of the cacao tree, which grows only in hot, humid regions close to the equator. Its scientific name, Theobroma, means 'food of the gods'. The tree was first cultivated in Central America more than three thousand years ago, and for most of its history chocolate was not eaten but drunk.

      B The Maya and later the Aztecs prepared a bitter, foaming drink from roasted cacao seeds, water, chilli and maize. It was reserved largely for rulers, warriors and priests. Cacao beans were so valuable that the Aztecs used them as money: according to one sixteenth-century record, a turkey cost a hundred beans and a tomato one.

      C Spanish conquerors took cacao back to Europe in the 1500s. There the chilli was replaced with sugar and the drink was served hot, and for the next two centuries chocolate was a fashionable luxury of the wealthy. The transformation into a solid food came with the Industrial Revolution. In 1828 a Dutch chemist, Coenraad van Houten, invented a press that separated cocoa butter from the bean, leaving a fine powder. In 1847 the English firm Fry's mixed cocoa powder, sugar and melted cocoa butter to produce the first chocolate bar, and in 1875 the Swiss Daniel Peter added condensed milk to create milk chocolate.

      D Turning cacao into chocolate is a long process. The seeds grow inside large pods, surrounded by a sweet white pulp. After harvest they are heaped up, covered with banana leaves and left to ferment for about a week; without this stage they would never develop the flavour of chocolate. They are then dried in the sun, shipped, roasted and ground. The smoothness of modern chocolate is due to a Swiss manufacturer, Rodolphe Lindt, who in 1879 found that stirring the liquid mixture for many hours removed its gritty texture. According to tradition he made the discovery by accident, having left a machine running over a weekend.

      E Part of the pleasure of chocolate is a matter of physics. Cocoa butter melts at about thirty-four degrees, just below the temperature of the human body, so a piece that is solid in the hand turns liquid in the mouth. Chocolate also contains a mild stimulant related to caffeine. Humans cope with it easily, but dogs break it down very slowly, and a bar of dark chocolate can make a small dog seriously ill.

      F Consumption is highest not in the countries that grow cacao but in northern Europe. The Swiss eat around ten kilograms per person each year, more than any other nation. Claims that chocolate is good for the heart should be treated with caution: the beneficial substances in cocoa are largely destroyed in processing, and much of the research has been paid for by manufacturers.

      G Today about two thirds of the world's cocoa comes from West Africa, chiefly Ivory Coast and Ghana, where it is grown mostly on small family farms. Many farmers earn very little, and the use of child labour on some farms has been widely criticised. Certification schemes that promise farmers a fairer price have grown, though they still cover only part of the market.

      A Rice is the staple food of more than half of humanity. It was domesticated in China, in the valley of the Yangtze River, around nine thousand years ago, and today roughly ninety per cent of the world's crop is still grown and eaten in Asia.

      B Most rice is grown in flooded fields called paddies. The plant does not actually need to stand in water, but it tolerates flooding, whereas most weeds do not, so the water acts as a natural weedkiller. Traditionally the seedlings are raised in a nursery and then transplanted by hand into the mud, a task demanding great labour. In mountainous regions farmers have carved steep hillsides into terraces to hold the water; those in the northern Philippines are some two thousand years old.

      C In the 1960s many experts predicted famine in Asia, as populations were growing faster than harvests. The disaster was avoided largely thanks to plant breeders at the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines. In 1966 they released a variety known as IR8. Traditional rice plants were tall, and when given fertiliser they grew top-heavy and fell over. IR8 had a short, stiff stem and could convert fertiliser into grain, so that yields doubled or even tripled. It became known as 'miracle rice' and was a central part of what was called the Green Revolution.

      D The institute also guards the raw material for future improvements. Its gene bank holds seeds of more than 130,000 kinds of rice, stored at minus twenty degrees in an earthquake-proof building. The value of the collection was shown in Cambodia. During the war and famine of the 1970s, farmers there ate their seed grain, and many traditional varieties vanished from the fields. Fortunately, samples had been collected a few years earlier, and in the 1980s the institute was able to send back seeds of several hundred Cambodian varieties.

      E One modern variety has been the subject of fierce argument. Hundreds of thousands of children in poor countries go blind each year because their diet lacks vitamin A. In 2000 scientists announced that they had added genes to rice that cause the grain to produce the substance from which the body makes the vitamin, giving it a yellow colour; it was named Golden Rice. Opponents of genetically modified crops campaigned against it for two decades, and it was not approved for planting until 2021, in the Philippines.

      F The place of rice in Asian life goes far beyond nutrition. In Chinese, Thai and several other languages, the everyday greeting was traditionally a question meaning 'Have you eaten rice?', and the same word serves for rice and for a meal. Emperors of Japan still plant and harvest a small field in the palace grounds each year.

      G New challenges have since appeared. Flooded paddies release methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, and rice farming consumes a large share of Asia's fresh water. Researchers are testing methods in which fields are allowed to dry out periodically, which saves water and cuts emissions. Others have developed varieties that survive two weeks under water, a valuable quality in areas where floods are becoming more frequent.

      A The bicycle seems such a simple machine that it is surprising how late it appeared. Its ancestor was the 'running machine' built in 1817 by the German baron Karl von Drais: two wheels joined by a wooden frame, which the rider pushed along with his feet on the ground. Some historians link the invention to the crop failures of 1816, which had led to the deaths of many horses.

      B Pedals were attached to the front wheel in France in the 1860s. The result, with its iron tyres, was so uncomfortable that it was nicknamed the 'boneshaker'. Since each turn of the pedals turned the wheel once, the only way to go faster was to enlarge the front wheel, and so the high-wheeler, or penny-farthing, appeared in the 1870s. It was fast but dangerous: a small stone could throw the rider head first to the ground.

      C The breakthrough was the 'safety bicycle' of 1885, designed by the Englishman John Kemp Starley. It had two wheels of equal size and a chain driving the rear wheel, essentially the design used today. Three years later John Dunlop, a Scottish vet living in Belfast, developed the air-filled tyre to make his son's tricycle more comfortable.

      D The effect on society was enormous. For the first time ordinary people had an affordable means of travelling beyond walking distance, to find work or simply for pleasure. The bicycle was especially significant for women, giving them new independence and encouraging more practical clothing; the American campaigner Susan B. Anthony said it had done more to free women than anything else in the world. Cyclists' demands for smoother roads also prepared the way, ironically, for the motor car.

      E The bicycle also gave birth to one of the world's great sporting events. In 1903 a struggling French sports newspaper, looking for a way to increase its sales, organised a race around the whole country. Sixty riders set out on the first Tour de France, covering more than 2,400 kilometres in six enormous stages, some of which continued through the night. The winner was a former chimney sweep. The newspaper's circulation more than doubled, and the yellow jersey later awarded to the race leader took its colour from the paper on which it was printed.

      F For much of the twentieth century the bicycle seemed to be in retreat, pushed off the roads by motor traffic. The country now most closely associated with cycling shows that this was not inevitable. In the early 1970s the Netherlands was as dominated by cars as its neighbours, and more than four hundred children were killed on its roads in a single year. Mass protests by parents persuaded the government to build a national network of separate cycle paths. Today more than a quarter of all journeys there are made by bicycle.

      G The newest chapter is electric. A small motor that assists the rider's pedalling makes hills and headwinds easy and allows older people and commuters with long journeys to cycle. Electric bicycles now outsell electric cars many times over worldwide. Surveys suggest that their owners are not lazier than other cyclists: they ride more often and further, and so get as much exercise in total.

      A Glass is made mainly from one of the commonest substances on Earth: sand. When sand is heated to a very high temperature with soda and lime, it melts, and on cooling it hardens without forming crystals, which is why it is transparent. Nature produces glass too. Obsidian, formed when volcanic lava cools quickly, was shaped into razor-sharp blades by Stone Age people.

      B Humans began making glass more than four thousand years ago in Mesopotamia and Egypt, at first as beads and small bottles formed around a core of clay. The crucial advance came in the first century BC, probably on the coast of what is now Syria and Lebanon: glass-blowing. By blowing air through a hollow tube into a ball of molten glass, a craftsman could make a vessel in minutes. Glass became cheap enough for ordinary Roman households.

      C In the Middle Ages the finest glass came from Venice. In 1291 the city ordered all its glassmakers to move to the island of Murano, officially to reduce the risk of fire, but also to keep their techniques secret. Craftsmen were forbidden to leave the republic.

      D A persistent myth holds that glass is really a very slow liquid, and that the windows of old cathedrals are thicker at the bottom because the glass has flowed downwards over the centuries. It is true that the panes are uneven, but the cause is the way they were made. Medieval glassmakers spun a blob of molten glass into a disc, which was always thicker in some places than others, and builders usually set the heavier edge at the bottom. Measurements show that at ordinary temperatures glass would not flow visibly in billions of years.

      E The greatest weakness of glass, its tendency to shatter into sharp pieces, was overcome by accident. In 1903 a French chemist, Edouard Benedictus, knocked a glass flask off a shelf and was surprised to find that, although it cracked, it kept its shape. The flask had contained a liquid plastic, which had dried to a thin film on the inside. From this observation he developed safety glass, in which a plastic sheet is sandwiched between two layers of glass. It was used in the eyepieces of gas masks during the First World War and afterwards in the windscreens of cars.

      F The screens of mobile phones depend on another kind of strengthened glass. It is dipped in a bath of hot chemicals, which forces larger atoms into the surface and squeezes it so tightly that scratches and cracks cannot easily spread. The material was invented in the 1960s but found few buyers and was abandoned, until a phone manufacturer asked for a tough, thin screen in 2007.

      G It is hard to overstate how much modern life owes to this material. Spectacles, invented in Italy around 1290, extended the working lives of scholars and craftsmen. Lenses made possible the telescope and the microscope, and hence modern astronomy and biology; the glass test tube and thermometer were essential to chemistry. Large flat windows became possible in 1959, when the British firm Pilkington perfected a method of floating molten glass on a bath of liquid tin. Today, strands of ultra-pure glass thinner than a hair carry almost all of the world's internet traffic as pulses of light.

      A It is difficult to imagine arithmetic without zero, yet for most of history people managed without it. The Babylonians, around 300 BC, used a pair of slanted marks to show an empty place within a number, rather as we distinguish 205 from 25, but they never treated it as a number in itself. The Maya of Central America independently invented a similar symbol, shaped like a shell, for their calendar.

      B The ancient Greeks, for all their brilliance in geometry, were uncomfortable with the notion. How, their philosophers asked, can nothing be something? The Romans had no zero either, and anyone who has tried to multiply using Roman numerals will understand the difficulty this caused.

      C Zero as a true number, which can be added, subtracted and multiplied like any other, appeared in India. In AD 628 the mathematician Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with it, stating for example that a number minus itself is zero. From India the system of nine digits and zero passed to the Islamic world. In ninth-century Baghdad the scholar al-Khwarizmi, who was born in the region of Khorezm in present-day Uzbekistan, wrote an influential book explaining it; the word 'algorithm' comes from the Latin form of his name. The Arabic word for zero, sifr, meaning 'empty', gave English both 'zero' and 'cipher'.

      D Even Brahmagupta was defeated by one question: what happens when a number is divided by zero? He suggested that zero divided by zero is zero, and later Indian mathematicians proposed that any other number divided by zero gives infinity. Modern mathematics simply declares the operation undefined. Computers must be told to avoid it, and the consequences of forgetting can be serious. In 1997 an American warship came to a halt at sea for more than two hours after a crew member entered a zero into a database and the ship's control software attempted to divide by it.

      E The absence of zero in early Europe has left a curious mark on the calendar. The system of counting years from the birth of Christ was devised by a monk in Rome in AD 525, long before the new numerals arrived. He began his count with the year one, and so the year 1 BC is followed immediately by AD 1, with nothing in between. This is why purists insisted that the third millennium began on 1 January 2001, a year after most of the world had celebrated.

      F Zero came fully into its own with the computer. In 1703 the German philosopher Gottfried Leibniz described a way of writing any number using only two symbols, 0 and 1. He regarded it mainly as a mathematical curiosity. Two and a half centuries later, engineers recognised that the two digits could be represented by a switch that is either off or on, and binary arithmetic became the language of every digital machine.

      G Europe was slow to accept the new numbers. The Italian merchant's son Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, promoted them in a book of 1202, having learned them in North Africa. Some authorities remained suspicious; Florence banned them from official accounts in 1299, fearing that a zero could easily be altered into a six or a nine. Only with the spread of printing did they finally replace Roman numerals.

      A Does the colour of a room change how we feel? Does a red shirt help an athlete to win? Popular books give confident answers, but the scientific evidence is more mixed.

      B Some effects appear to be real. In a study of the 2004 Olympic Games, researchers examined combat sports such as boxing and wrestling, in which competitors were randomly given red or blue clothing. Those in red won about fifty-five per cent of the contests, an advantage that was greatest when opponents were evenly matched. The researchers suggested that red is a natural signal of dominance, as it is in many animals. In other experiments, students who briefly saw the colour red before a test performed slightly worse on problems requiring flexible thinking, perhaps because red is associated with danger and with teachers' corrections.

      C Many common claims, however, rest on little evidence. In the late 1970s a particular shade of pink was reported to calm aggressive prisoners, and some jails painted cells with it. Later, better-controlled studies failed to confirm any lasting effect.

      D Culture complicates matters further. White is the colour of weddings in Western countries, whereas in China and India it is traditionally worn at funerals. Red suggests danger to many Europeans but good fortune in China. Even the boundaries between colours vary: Russian has two separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, and experiments show that Russian speakers are slightly quicker than English speakers at telling apart shades that fall on either side of that line.

      E The meanings attached to colours have often been a matter of cost. In the ancient Mediterranean the most prized dye was a purple extracted from sea snails; some ten thousand of them were needed to produce a single gram, and in Rome only the emperor was permitted to wear a robe dyed entirely with it. Purple remained the colour of rank until 1856, when an eighteen-year-old chemistry student in London, William Perkin, attempting to make a medicine for malaria, produced instead a dark sludge that stained cloth a brilliant mauve. It was the first synthetic dye, and within a few years purple dresses were within reach of any shop assistant.

      F Conventions that seem natural can be surprisingly recent. The rule that pink is for girls and blue for boys dates only from about the 1940s. Earlier in the century American shops and magazines were divided on the question, and some gave exactly the opposite advice, on the grounds that pink, a paler version of red, was the stronger and more decided colour, while blue was delicate and dainty.

      G It should not be forgotten that people do not all see the same colours. About one man in twelve, and one woman in two hundred, has difficulty in telling red from green. For this reason designers are advised never to rely on colour alone to convey important information. Traffic lights are a good example: the red lamp is always at the top, so that a driver who cannot distinguish the colours can still read the signal by its position.

      H Asked for their favourite colour, people in most countries surveyed choose blue. Researchers think the reason is simple: we tend to like colours associated with things we like, such as clear skies and clean water.

      A People have always wondered about the meaning of dreams. In the ancient world they were commonly taken to be messages from the gods or glimpses of the future. In 1900 the Austrian doctor Sigmund Freud proposed a different interpretation: dreams, he argued, are disguised expressions of wishes that we hide even from ourselves.

      B Scientific study of dreaming became possible in 1953, when researchers at the University of Chicago noticed that sleepers' eyes move rapidly beneath their lids at certain periods of the night. Volunteers woken during this rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep nearly always reported a vivid dream. During REM the brain is almost as active as when awake, yet the muscles of the body are effectively paralysed, which prevents us from acting out our dreams. We now know that some dreaming occurs in other stages of sleep as well.

      C There is still no agreed explanation of what dreams are for. One influential theory, put forward in 1977, holds that they have no purpose at all: the sleeping brain produces random signals, and the thinking part of the brain does its best to turn them into a story. Others believe that dreaming helps to process memories and emotions. People deprived of REM sleep are worse at learning new skills, and experiments show that the brain replays recent experiences during sleep. A further idea is that dreams are rehearsals. A large proportion involve being chased or threatened, and practising such situations in safety might have helped our ancestors to survive.

      D What do people actually dream about? The American psychologist Calvin Hall spent more than thirty years collecting written accounts of dreams, eventually assembling over 50,000. They proved far less exotic than might be expected. Most dreams took place in ordinary surroundings such as a house or a street, and involved the dreamer's family, friends and colleagues. Unpleasant feelings were considerably more common than pleasant ones, anxiety being the most frequent of all.

      E People who have been blind from birth dream as often as anyone else, but their dreams contain no pictures: they are composed of sounds, touch, smell and movement. Those who lost their sight after the age of about seven usually continue to see in their dreams for the rest of their lives. Animals, too, appear to dream. When researchers recorded the brain cells of rats that had spent the day learning a maze, they found that the same cells fired in the same order while the animals slept, as though they were running the route again.

      F Dreams have occasionally been credited with real achievements. The German chemist August Kekule claimed that the ring-shaped structure of an important chemical came to him in 1865 after he dozed by the fire and saw a snake seizing its own tail. A century later the musician Paul McCartney woke one morning with a complete melody in his head and at first assumed that he must have heard it somewhere. It became the song 'Yesterday'.

      G Most dreams are forgotten within minutes of waking. A few people, however, experience lucid dreams, in which they are aware of dreaming and can sometimes direct what happens, an ability that researchers have confirmed in the laboratory.

      A The Olympic Games were first held, according to tradition, in 776 BC at Olympia in southern Greece, as part of a religious festival in honour of the god Zeus. At the earliest Games there was a single event, a sprint of about 190 metres. Wrestling, boxing, chariot racing and other contests were added later. Only free Greek men could compete, and married women were not even permitted to watch. Winners received no medals, only a wreath of olive leaves, but their home cities rewarded them generously. A sacred truce allowed athletes and spectators to travel safely through warring states.

      B The Games were held every four years for more than a millennium, until they were abolished at the end of the fourth century AD by a Christian Roman emperor who regarded them as pagan.

      C Their revival was the work of a French aristocrat, Pierre de Coubertin, who believed that sport built character and that international competition could promote peace. The first modern Games took place in Athens in 1896, with about 240 athletes, all of them men, from fourteen countries. Women first took part in Paris in 1900. The marathon, incidentally, was a modern invention, inspired by the legend of a messenger who ran to Athens with news of a victory.

      D Several features that seem ancient are in fact modern inventions. The curious length of the marathon, 42.195 kilometres, was fixed at the London Games of 1908, when the course was laid out to start beneath the windows of Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal seats in the stadium. The relay of runners carrying a flame from Olympia to the host city was devised for the Berlin Games of 1936. Even gold medals are not what they appear: since 1912 they have been made of silver covered with a thin layer of gold.

      E The Games have also been a stage for moments that had little to do with sport. At Berlin, the government of the day intended the event to demonstrate its ideas of racial superiority, and was embarrassed when the black American athlete Jesse Owens won four gold medals. In 1960 the Ethiopian runner Abebe Bikila won the marathon in Rome running barefoot through the streets, the first African from south of the Sahara to become an Olympic champion.

      F A parallel movement began in an English hospital. Ludwig Guttmann, a doctor treating soldiers with injuries to the spine, was convinced that sport would restore their strength and confidence. On the day the London Olympics opened in 1948, he held an archery contest for sixteen patients in wheelchairs. The event became annual, then international, and in 1960 the first Paralympic Games took place in Rome with four hundred competitors. More than four thousand now take part.

      G The Games have grown enormously since then: more than 10,000 athletes from over 200 teams now take part in the summer event. Growth has brought problems. Coubertin's ideal of amateur competition has given way to professionalism, the Games have repeatedly been disrupted by political boycotts, and scandals over banned drugs are frequent. The cost of hosting has also soared, and fewer cities are now willing to bid.

      Host: Hello and welcome back to The Slow Traveller, the podcast for people who think the journey matters as much as the destination. I'm Kate, and this week I'm answering your questions about seeing Europe by train.

      Host: The question I get most often is about rail passes. Are they worth it? The honest answer is, it depends. A pass gives you unlimited travel in thirty-three countries, and for people under twenty-eight it's about a quarter cheaper. If you're planning lots of long journeys in a short time, it saves money. But if you only want three or four trips, ordinary tickets booked early are usually cheaper.

      Host: And booking early really matters. Tickets for most high-speed trains go on sale about three months ahead, and the lowest prices disappear quickly. One thing people forget is that even with a pass, you often need a seat reservation on fast trains. In France and Spain that's compulsory.

      Host: My second tip is to try a night train. They're coming back all over Europe. You fall asleep in Vienna and wake up in Rome, and you save the cost of a hotel. I'd pay a little extra for a bed in a sleeping compartment rather than an ordinary seat. Trust me, your back will thank you.

      Host: Third, pack light. You'll be lifting your bag onto racks and carrying it up station stairs. I travel with one backpack of about nine kilos, and I've never wished I had more.

      Host: What about food? Station restaurants are expensive. Do what locals do and buy bread, cheese and fruit at a market before you board. A picnic by the window is one of the great pleasures of train travel.

      Host: Finally, leave time for connections. I allow at least forty minutes when changing trains, because delays happen, especially in summer.

      Host: My favourite route? The line through the Swiss Alps from Chur to Tirano. It crosses nearly two hundred bridges, and every one has a view.

      Host: Next week, travelling with children. Until then, enjoy the ride.

      Ranger: There are three marked trails starting from this centre. The Blue Trail is the easiest. It's a four-kilometre circle around the lake, it's flat, and it takes about an hour. It's suitable for pushchairs.

      Ranger: The Red Trail climbs through the forest to a waterfall. It's seven kilometres there and back, and you should allow three hours. The last section is rocky, so you need proper walking boots.

      Ranger: The Black Trail goes to the summit of Stonepeak itself. That's a full day, at least seven hours, and it's only for experienced walkers. If you choose it, please write your name in the book at the desk before you leave, and sign again when you return.

      Ranger: Whichever trail you take, remember that the weather changes quickly here. Carry a waterproof jacket, plenty of water and something to eat. Mobile phones don't work in most of the park, so take a paper map. We sell them here for two pounds fifty.

      Ranger: A few rules. Fires are forbidden everywhere, because the forest is very dry this summer. Please take all your litter home. Dogs must be kept on a lead between March and July, when birds are nesting on the ground.

      Ranger: Camping is allowed only at the official site by the lake, which costs twelve pounds a night. You need to book at this desk.

      Ranger: This centre has an exhibition about the park's wildlife and a café. We close at five thirty. And at eight this evening there's a guided walk to look for bats. It's free, but bring a torch.

      Guide: The castle was attacked many times but captured only once, in thirteen thirty-two, after its defenders ran out of food.       Emma: Jack, we need to finalise the design of our experiment today. The proposal is due on Monday.

      Jack: I know. So we're testing whether a short sleep after learning improves memory, right?

      Emma: Yes. I think we should keep it simple. Two groups. Everyone learns a list of word pairs, then one group has a nap and the other stays awake.

      Jack: How long should the nap be?

      Emma: The studies I read used ninety minutes, but that's too long for volunteers to give up. I'd say twenty minutes.

      Jack: Would that be enough to show an effect?

      Emma: One paper found an improvement after only six minutes, so I think so.

      Jack: OK. And what does the other group do during that time?

      Emma: That's the tricky part. If they use their phones, they'll be learning new things, which might interfere. I suggest they watch a nature film with no speech.

      Jack: Good idea. How many participants do we need?

      Emma: Doctor Lewis said at least forty, so twenty in each group.

      Jack: We should put them in groups at random, not let them choose. Otherwise all the tired people will choose the nap.

      Emma: Exactly. We could toss a coin for each person.

      Jack: Where can people sleep, though? The psychology lab is so noisy.

      Emma: I asked about that. We can use the quiet room in the library, as long as we book it a week ahead.

      Jack: Great. And what time of day?

      Emma: Early afternoon, about two o'clock. That's when people naturally feel sleepy.

      Jack: Should we test them straight after the nap?

      Emma: I'd wait ten minutes, so they're properly awake. People are often confused just after waking.

      Jack: Fine. What about the ethics form?

      Emma: We must tell participants not to drive straight afterwards, in case they still feel sleepy. And nobody under eighteen can take part.

      Jack: I'll write the method section if you do the introduction.

      Emma: Deal. Send me your part by Saturday.

      2 Early postal systems were only for use ✔ government

      4 Rowland Hill worked as a ✔ teacher

      Транскрипт (открывай только после проверки)

      Lecturer: Today I want to look at something we tend to take for granted, the postal service, and to show how it shaped modern communication.

      Lecturer: Organised systems for carrying messages are extremely old. The Persian Empire, around five hundred BC, had a royal road with stations where riders changed horses. A message could cross the empire in about a week. But this system, like the later Roman one, was for government use only. Ordinary people had to rely on travellers or merchants to carry their letters.

      Lecturer: Public postal services developed in Europe from the sixteenth century, but they were expensive and complicated. In Britain before eighteen forty, the cost of a letter depended on the distance and on the number of sheets of paper. And, importantly, the cost was paid not by the sender but by the person who received it. Many people simply refused to accept letters they could not afford.

      Lecturer: The reform came from a teacher called Rowland Hill. In eighteen thirty-seven he published a pamphlet arguing that the real cost of carrying a letter was tiny, and that most of the expense came from calculating and collecting the charges. He proposed a single low price of one penny for any distance, paid in advance by the sender. To show payment, he suggested a small piece of paper with glue on the back. This was the first postage stamp, known as the Penny Black, issued in May eighteen forty.

      Lecturer: The results were dramatic. Within a year the number of letters sent in Britain more than doubled. Other countries copied the system quickly. Cheap post encouraged people to learn to read and write, helped businesses to grow, and allowed families separated by migration to stay in contact.

      Lecturer: In eighteen seventy-four, an international agreement signed in Switzerland created what is now the Universal Postal Union, so that a stamp bought in one country would carry a letter to any other. Today, of course, the number of letters is falling because of email, but parcels are increasing rapidly as a result of online shopping.

      You will hear part of a lecture on animal behaviour.

      mp3

      Complete the notes. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

      1 Von Frisch began his experiments in the ✔ 1920s/nineteen twenties
      2 He marked bees with small spots of ✔ paint
      3 The round dance means food is within about metres ✔ 50/fifty
      4 The round dance does not show ✔ direction
      5 One second of waggling represents about one ✔ kilometre/kilometer/km
      6 In the hive, bees use to represent the sun ✔ gravity
      7 Other bees touch the dancer with their ✔ antennae
      8 Von Frisch shared the Nobel Prize in ✔ 1973/nineteen seventy-three
      9 Later experiments used small devices fixed to bees ✔ radar
      10 Bees also dance when choosing a new ✔ home
      Транскрипт (открывай только после проверки)

      Lecturer: In this lecture I'd like to describe one of the most remarkable communication systems in the animal world, the dance of the honeybee.

      Lecturer: Beekeepers had noticed for centuries that when one bee found a rich source of food, many others soon arrived at the same place. The explanation was discovered by an Austrian scientist, Karl von Frisch, who began his experiments in the nineteen twenties. He marked individual bees with tiny spots of paint and watched them through a glass wall in the hive.

      Lecturer: He found that a bee returning from flowers close to the hive performs what he called the round dance. She simply runs in circles. This tells the others that food is nearby, within about fifty metres, but it gives no direction.

      Lecturer: For food that is farther away, the bee performs the waggle dance. She runs in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run. The two key pieces of information are in that straight run. First, its length shows the distance. Roughly speaking, one second of waggling means one kilometre. Second, the angle of the run shows the direction. Inside the dark hive the bee dances on a vertical surface, and she uses gravity to represent the sun. A run straight up means fly towards the sun. A run at sixty degrees to the right of vertical means fly sixty degrees to the right of the sun.

      Lecturer: The other bees follow the dancer closely, touching her with their antennae, and they also learn the smell of the flowers from her body.

      Lecturer: Many scientists at first refused to believe that an insect could use such a symbolic language. Von Frisch's ideas were only fully accepted decades later, and he shared the Nobel Prize in nineteen seventy-three. Later experiments using tiny radar devices attached to bees confirmed that they really do fly to the place the dance indicates.

      Lecturer: Bees also use the dance when choosing a new home. Scouts dance to advertise sites they have found, and the colony moves only when enough scouts agree. It is, in effect, a kind of democratic vote.

      You will hear part of a lecture on the history of world trade.

      mp3

      Complete the notes. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

      1 Before containers, loading could make up of a voyage's cost ✔ half
      2 Another common problem in ports was ✔ theft
      3 McLean's business was in ✔ trucking
      4 The Ideal X carried containers ✔ 58/fifty-eight
      5 Loading cost fell to about cents a ton ✔ 16/sixteen
      6 Dock workers went on ✔ strike
      7 Standard container lengths are twenty and feet ✔ 40/forty
      8 Factories moved especially to East ✔ Asia
      9 About per cent of non-bulk goods travel in containers ✔ 90/ninety
      10 In 2021 a ship blocked the Suez Canal for days ✔ 6/six
      Транскрипт (открывай только после проверки)

      Lecturer: When we talk about globalisation, we usually think of the internet or of trade agreements. Today I want to argue that a simple steel box has been just as important.

      Lecturer: Until the nineteen fifties, loading a ship was slow and costly. Goods arrived at the port in sacks, barrels and wooden crates of every size. Each item had to be carried on board by hand and packed carefully into the ship. A vessel could spend more time in port than at sea, and loading could account for half the total cost of a voyage. Theft was common too.

      Lecturer: The man who changed this was not a sailor but an American trucking businessman, Malcolm McLean. He asked a simple question. Why unload the truck at all? Why not lift the whole body of the truck onto the ship? On the twenty-sixth of April nineteen fifty-six, his converted oil tanker, the Ideal X, sailed from New Jersey to Texas carrying fifty-eight containers. The cost of loading fell from nearly six dollars a ton to about sixteen cents.

      Lecturer: Success was not immediate. Ports needed huge new cranes, and dock workers, who feared for their jobs, went on strike. Above all, different companies used boxes of different sizes. Only in the nineteen sixties were international standards agreed, the most common being lengths of twenty and forty feet. Standard boxes could move from ship to train to truck anywhere in the world.

      Lecturer: The consequences were enormous. Transport became so cheap that it made sense to manufacture goods thousands of kilometres from the customer. Factories moved to countries with lower wages, especially in East Asia. Old ports in city centres, such as London and New York, declined, because container ships needed deep water and a great deal of space. New ports like Rotterdam and Singapore grew rapidly.

      Lecturer: Today about ninety per cent of non-bulk goods travel in containers, and the largest ships carry more than twenty thousand of them. The system is efficient but also fragile, as we saw in twenty twenty-one, when a single ship blocked the Suez Canal for six days and delayed trade around the world.

      mp3

      2 The temperature difference is greatest at ✔ night
      3 At night, a city centre can be up to degrees warmer ✔ 10/ten
      4 Dark surfaces such as absorb sunlight ✔ asphalt
      5 Trees cool the air by giving and releasing water ✔ shade
      6 Tall buildings trap heat and block the ✔ wind
      7 Air conditioners pump outside ✔ heat

      9 A white roof can be degrees cooler than a black one ✔ 30/thirty
      10 Melbourne plans to nearly its tree cover ✔ double
      Транскрипт (открывай только после проверки)

      Lecturer: Good morning. Today's topic is a problem that affects more than half of the world's population, the urban heat island.

      Lecturer: The term describes the fact that cities are warmer than the countryside around them. The effect was first measured in London in the early nineteenth century by an amateur scientist called Luke Howard, who compared thermometer readings in the centre with those in nearby villages. Today the difference in a large city is typically between one and three degrees during the day. But the important point is that it is greatest at night, when a city centre can be as much as ten degrees warmer than the surrounding fields.

      Lecturer: Why does this happen? There are four main causes. First, materials. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roof tiles absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly after sunset. Second, the lack of plants. Trees cool the air, both by giving shade and by releasing water through their leaves. Third, the shape of cities. Tall buildings on narrow streets trap heat and block the wind. And fourth, waste heat from vehicles, factories and, ironically, air conditioners, which cool the inside of a building by pumping heat outside.

      Lecturer: The consequences are serious. During heat waves the death rate rises, especially among elderly people, because the body cannot recover when nights stay hot. Demand for electricity increases sharply, and air quality gets worse.

      Lecturer: What can be done? The cheapest solution is to change the colour of surfaces. A white roof reflects most of the sunlight that falls on it, and can be thirty degrees cooler than a black one. New York has painted more than a million square metres of roofs white.

      Lecturer: Planting trees is the second approach. Studies show that a street with mature trees can be several degrees cooler than one without. The city of Melbourne plans to almost double its tree cover by twenty forty.

      Lecturer: Green roofs, covered with soil and plants, are a third option, though they cost more to build. Next week we'll look at how planners are using these ideas.

      You will hear part of a lecture about the history of an everyday object.

      mp3

      Complete the notes. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

      1 Graphite was found near the village of Borrowdale in the fifteen ✔ sixties/60s
      2 It was first used for marking ✔ sheep
      3 People wrongly believed the material was ✔ lead
      4 Early graphite sticks were wrapped in or sheepskin ✔ string
      5 Conte's method was developed in the year ✔ 1795/seventeen ninety-five
      6 He mixed powdered graphite with ✔ clay
      7 More clay makes a pencil ✔ harder
      8 In 1858 a was attached to the end of the pencil ✔ rubber
      9 In China, yellow was associated with ✔ royalty
      10 One pencil can draw a line about kilometres long ✔ 56/fifty-six
      Транскрипт (открывай только после проверки)

      Lecturer: In this series on everyday technology, I want to turn today to an object so ordinary that we hardly notice it, the pencil.

      Lecturer: Its story begins in the north of England in the fifteen sixties. According to tradition, a storm blew down a large tree near the village of Borrowdale, and under its roots shepherds found a black, shiny substance. They discovered it was excellent for marking their sheep. People believed the material was a kind of lead, which is why we still talk about the lead of a pencil. In fact it was graphite, a form of carbon, and pencils have never contained any lead at all.

      Lecturer: The Borrowdale graphite was unusually pure and solid. It could be cut into thin sticks, which at first were wrapped in string or sheepskin, and later placed inside a wooden case. For two centuries England had almost a monopoly, and the graphite was so valuable that it was transported under armed guard.

      Lecturer: The modern pencil was born out of war. In the seventeen nineties France was fighting Britain and could no longer import English graphite. An officer in the French army, Nicolas Conte, was asked to find a solution. In seventeen ninety-five he mixed powdered graphite of poor quality with clay, formed the mixture into rods and baked them in an oven. The method had an unexpected advantage. By changing the amount of clay, he could make the pencil harder or softer. More clay gives a harder, lighter line. That is the origin of the grades we still use, such as H for hard and B for black.

      Lecturer: Two later improvements came from America. In eighteen fifty-eight Hymen Lipman patented a pencil with a rubber attached to the end. And the familiar yellow colour appeared in eighteen ninety. The best graphite then came from China, where yellow was associated with royalty, so manufacturers painted their finest pencils yellow as a sign of quality.

      Lecturer: Why has the pencil survived the computer age? It is cheap, it needs no battery, and it works upside down, under water and even in space. A single pencil can draw a line roughly fifty-six kilometres long.

      Lecturer: When we think about why writing was invented, we imagine poetry, or laws, or letters. The truth is less romantic. Writing was invented by accountants.

      Lecturer: The story begins in Mesopotamia, in what is now southern Iraq. By about three thousand three hundred BC the city of Uruk had perhaps forty thousand inhabitants, and its temples controlled huge stores of grain, sheep and beer. Somebody had to keep records.

      Lecturer: For thousands of years before this, people in the region had used small clay tokens for counting. One shape stood for a measure of grain, another for a jar of oil. To prevent cheating, the tokens for a delivery were sealed inside a hollow clay ball. The problem, of course, was that you had to break the ball to check what was in it. So people began pressing the tokens into the outside of the ball before sealing it. And eventually someone realised that the marks alone were enough. The ball became a flat tablet, and the tokens were no longer needed.

      Lecturer: The first signs were simple pictures. A head of barley meant barley. But pictures are slow to draw in wet clay, so scribes began pressing the end of a cut reed into the surface instead. This made marks shaped like wedges. The Latin word for wedge is cuneus, and so we call the script cuneiform.

      Lecturer: The next step was the decisive one. Signs began to represent sounds as well as things. This allowed scribes to write names and, eventually, whole sentences of the spoken language. Then it was forgotten completely, until scholars deciphered it in the nineteenth century. Because clay survives fire, hundreds of thousands of tablets still exist, most of them, I'm afraid, receipts.

      Lecturer: A desert is defined as a region that receives less than two hundred and fifty millimetres of rain a year. For a plant, that creates one overwhelming problem, how to obtain water and how to keep it. Today I'll describe three strategies that desert plants have evolved.

      Lecturer: The first strategy is storage, and the best-known example is the cactus. Look at a saguaro cactus from the deserts of Arizona. It has no leaves. Its spines are in fact leaves that have changed over millions of years. They lose almost no water, they protect the plant from thirsty animals, and they even provide a little shade. The stem of the saguaro is folded, like an accordion, so that it can expand. After a storm, a large plant can take up about seven hundred and fifty litres of water in a few days. Its roots are shallow, but they spread out as far as the plant is tall, to catch rain before it disappears.

      Lecturer: Cacti also breathe differently from other plants. Most plants open the tiny holes in their surface during the day to take in carbon dioxide, and they lose water as they do so. A cactus opens them only at night, when the air is cool, stores the gas, and uses it for photosynthesis the next day. The price is slow growth. A saguaro may be only a few centimetres tall after ten years, though it can live for two centuries.

      Lecturer: The second strategy is to reach water that other plants cannot. The mesquite tree sends its roots down to water lying deep underground. Roots have been found at depths of more than fifty metres.

      Lecturer: The third strategy is simply to avoid the dry season. Many small desert flowers live for only a few weeks. Their seeds can lie in the soil for years, protected by a chemical coat that prevents them from growing. Only heavy rain washes the chemical away. Then the desert suddenly turns into a carpet of colour, the plants flower, produce new seeds and die, all before the ground dries out again.

      Lecturer: Next time, we'll consider desert animals.

      Lecturer: If I asked you which invention made the modern city possible, you might say steel, or concrete. I'd like to suggest another candidate, the lift, or elevator.

      Lecturer: Lifting platforms are very old. The Romans used them in the Colosseum to raise animals into the arena. Nineteenth-century factories and warehouses had steam-powered lifts for goods. But nobody would travel in one by choice, for a simple reason. If the rope broke, the platform fell.

      Lecturer: The man who solved this was an American mechanic, Elisha Otis. He designed a safety brake, a spring that pushed metal teeth into the guide rails on each side if the rope lost its tension. In eighteen fifty-four, at a great exhibition in New York, he demonstrated it in dramatic style. He stood on a platform high above the crowd and ordered the rope to be cut. The platform dropped a few centimetres, and stopped.

      Lecturer: The first passenger lift using his brake was installed three years later in a department store in New York. It was a building of only five storeys, and the lift travelled at less than a kilometre an hour. But the principle was established.

      Lecturer: Consider what this meant for buildings. Before the lift, few were higher than six floors, because that was as far as people were willing to climb. And the top floors were the cheapest, occupied by servants and the poor. The lift turned that upside down. Suddenly the highest floors, with light, quiet and a view, became the most desirable and the most expensive.

      Lecturer: Height then depended on structure. Steel frames, first used in Chicago in the eighteen eighties, allowed walls to become thin. Electric lifts arrived in the same decade and were faster and cleaner than steam.

      Lecturer: Today's limits are different. In very tall buildings the steel cables become too heavy to support their own weight, which restricts a single lift to about five hundred metres. Engineers are now using cables of carbon fibre, which weigh far less. And in the tallest towers, lifts take up so much floor space that designers use double-deck cars, serving two floors at once.

      Host: Hello, and welcome to Curious Minds, the podcast that takes one small question and follows it wherever it leads. I'm Ben. This week's question came from a listener called Olivia, who is nine. She asked, why doesn't honey go bad?

      Host: It's a great question, because it really doesn't. Archaeologists opening Egyptian tombs have found pots of honey around three thousand years old, and it was still perfectly safe to eat.

      Host: So what's the secret? There are three parts to the answer. The first is water, or rather the lack of it. Honey is only about seventeen per cent water. Bacteria and moulds need moisture to grow, and when they land in honey the sugar actually pulls the water out of them, and they die.

      Host: The second reason is that honey is acidic. Its acidity is similar to that of orange juice, and most microbes can't survive in that.

      Host: The third reason is my favourite, because it involves the bees themselves. Nectar from flowers is mostly water, as much as eighty per cent. A bee collects it, carries it home in a special stomach and passes it to another bee, mouth to mouth. Appetising, I know. In the process the bees add an enzyme. That enzyme produces tiny amounts of hydrogen peroxide, the same chemical used to clean wounds. Then the bees fan the nectar with their wings to evaporate the water, and finally they seal each cell with wax.

      Host: That, by the way, explains why honey has been used as medicine for thousands of years. People put it on cuts and burns long before anyone knew what bacteria were, and some hospitals use a special medical honey today.

      Host: One warning. Honey only lasts if the jar is closed. Leave it open in a damp kitchen and it absorbs water from the air, and then it can spoil. And if your honey goes hard and cloudy, don't throw it out. It has only crystallised. Stand the jar in warm water and it will turn liquid again.

      Host: Finally, a number that changed how I look at my breakfast. In her whole life, a single worker bee makes about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey.

      Host: Welcome to Blue Planet Stories. I'm Tom, and today's episode is about one of the strangest scientific experiments ever carried out. Nobody planned it, and its equipment was made for the bath.

      Host: In January nineteen ninety-two, a container ship was crossing the Pacific Ocean from Hong Kong to the United States when it ran into a violent storm. Twelve containers were washed overboard. One of them broke open, and released about twenty-nine thousand plastic bath toys into the sea. There were yellow ducks, red beavers, blue turtles and green frogs.

      Host: Now, to most people that's a small accident. To an oceanographer called Curtis Ebbesmeyer, it was a gift. Scientists who study ocean currents normally release five hundred or a thousand floating bottles and hope that a few are found. Here were tens of thousands of bright objects, all released at a known place at a known time.

      Host: Ten months later, the first toys washed up on the coast of Alaska, about three thousand two hundred kilometres from where they had started. Ebbesmeyer built a network of people who walk beaches, and asked them to report every toy they found. With a colleague, he put the data into a computer model of the currents.

      Host: The model predicted that some of the toys would circle the North Pacific, and they did. That great circular current takes about three years to complete one round. Others, the model said, would drift north through the Bering Strait and become frozen in the Arctic ice.
